paper_context.research_question: Can automatically-generated sense inventories that prioritize substitutability improve lexical substitution rankings from vector- and embedding-based models, and how should such inventories be constructed to maximize coverage and substitutability?
contribution_type: novel clustering method for paraphrases by word sense
multi-view NMF approach incorporating four complementary views
sense filtering technique for post-hoc improvement of lexsub rankings
empirical comparison of sense inventory quality
contribution_style: problem reformulation (reframing lexsub as sense-filtering task)
methodological combination (multi-view clustering adapted for substitutability)
empirical validation with oracle and practical experiments
main_claims: Current state-of-the-art lexsub models ignore word sense but can be improved by filtering with high-quality sense inventories
Multi-view clustering incorporating context substitutability, paraphrase similarity, WordNet structure, and foreign translations produces more substitutable sense clusters than prior work
Automatically-generated sense inventories can exceed WordNet and PPDBClus in substitutability (B-Cubed F-Score) and improve lexsub performance when used as filters
B-Cubed F-Score is a valid metric for measuring sense inventory fitness for the lexsub task
A simple WSD method (best-fit sense selection) can approximate oracle performance in practical sense filtering
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Substitutability metric validity: correlation between B-Cubed F-Score and oracle GAP improvements
Sense inventory coverage: number of target words and paraphrases with assigned senses
Clustering quality: intrinsic measures (Silhouette Coefficient) and extrinsic measures (B-Cubed F-Score against human annotations)
Lexsub ranking improvement: oracle GAP and best-fit GAP scores across ranking models (Syn.VSM, AddCos)
Part-of-speech sensitivity: differential performance on nouns vs. other POS
Comparison to baselines: WordNet+, TWSI, PPDBClus across all metrics
View contribution analysis: ablation study showing impact of each clustering view
Practical applicability: gap between oracle and best-fit performance indicating WSD method effectiveness

extracted_claims.claim_label: SOTA lexsub models ignore sense but can be improved by filtering
extracted_claims.claim_text: Current state-of-the-art lexical substitution models ignore word sense, instead relying on powerful vector and embedded word representations to find good substitutes. These models can be improved by integrating word sense inventories to filter substitutes from the correct sense to the top of the rankings.
evidence: Current state-of-the-art models for lexical substitution ignore word sense (Abstract)
Many early lexsub models approached the problem in two steps: identify sense, then propose substitutes; but current SOTA systems ignore the sense disambiguation step altogether (lines 100-110)
Hypothesis: a high-coverage, substitutable sense inventory can be used in combination with a word-based lexsub model to improve the quality of proposed substitutes (lines 140-150)
uncertainty_flags: No explicit evidence provided that current SOTA models *cannot* implicitly capture sense distinctions through contextualized embeddings
Claim assumes sense filtering is the primary mechanism for improvement; alternative explanations (e.g., re-ranking bias) not ruled out

extracted_claims.claim_label: Multi-view clustering produces more substitutable sense clusters
extracted_claims.claim_text: Multi-view clustering incorporating context substitutability, paraphrase similarity, WordNet structure, and foreign translations produces sense clusters that are more substitutable and have wider coverage than existing sense inventories (WordNet+, PPDBClus, TWSI).
evidence: Abstract: 'Our method results in sense clusters that are more substitutable and have wider coverage than existing sense inventories.'
Section 4.3: 'all multi-view inventories and the SubstClusP single-view inventory are more substitutable than WordNet and TWSI in terms of B-Cubed F-Score'
Table 2: B3F0.5 scores show WordNet+ (0.841), TWSI (0.842), PPDBClus (0.736)
Table 5: Oracle GAP scores for SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM (0.675) and AddCos (0.671) exceed or match baselines
uncertainty_flags: B-Cubed F-Score superiority does not directly translate to lexsub performance improvement (Best-Fit GAP often lower than Oracle GAP)
Coverage metrics not explicitly reported in main results; claim of 'wider coverage' not quantified
Performance on nouns specifically is weaker than TWSI (acknowledged in Section 6), suggesting POS-dependent effectiveness

extracted_claims.claim_label: B-Cubed F-Score is valid metric for sense inventory fitness for lexsub
extracted_claims.claim_text: B-Cubed F-Score is a valid metric for measuring sense inventory fitness for the lexical substitution task, as it correlates with oracle GAP improvements.
evidence: Section 2: 'We propose a cluster quality metric, B-Cubed F-Score (Amigó et al., 2009), as a way of comparing an automatically-generated sense inventory against a human-generated set of substitutability judgements.'

Section 6: 'Comparing the B-Cubed F-Score for the sense inventories to the Oracle GAP scores, we find that our substitutability metric is generally a good indicator of the potential for a sense inventory to improve lexsub rankings.'
uncertainty_flags: Correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP is stated as 'generally' good but not quantified (no correlation coefficient provided)
Best-Fit GAP scores are explicitly stated as 'not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP scores' (Section 6), indicating metric limitations in practical settings
B3F0.5 uses β=0.5 to emphasize precision; sensitivity to β parameter choice not explored

extracted_claims.claim_label: Simple WSD method approximates oracle performance
extracted_claims.claim_text: A simple word sense disambiguation method (best-fit sense selection based on top-5 ranked substitutes) can approximate oracle performance in practical sense filtering for lexical substitution.
evidence: Section 5.4: 'For each target word in context, we choose the 'best-fit' sense to be the sense most frequently represented among the top-5 ranked substitutes by the lexsub ranking model.'
Section 6: 'in most cases, all sense inventories except PPDBClus can improve the GAP score when a simple WSD method is applied (Best-Fit GAP)'
uncertainty_flags: Gap between Oracle and Best-Fit GAP is substantial (e.g., SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM: 0.675 oracle vs 0.552 best-fit, a 0.123 difference)
Simple WSD method fails on nouns specifically (Section 6: 'The simple WSD method fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases')
No analysis of failure modes or conditions under which best-fit approximation breaks down
Method is heuristic (top-5 frequency); no justification for why this particular heuristic should work

extracted_claims.claim_label: Sense filtering improves lexsub rankings across models
extracted_claims.claim_text: Sense filtering using automatically-generated sense inventories can significantly improve lexical substitution rankings generated by existing vector- and embedding-based models (Syn.VSM, AddCos).
evidence: Table 5: Oracle GAP improvements across all sense inventories for both Syn.VSM and AddCos
Section 6: 'All baseline and clustered sense inventories can improve the GAP score of the Syn.VSM and AddCos ranking models when used as a filter, based on Oracle GAP scores.'
Example in Table 4: sense filtering improves GAP from 0.47 to 0.78 for target 'year'
uncertainty_flags: Oracle experiment assumes perfect sense knowledge; practical Best-Fit improvements are much smaller and inconsistent
Improvement magnitude varies widely by sense inventory and model (e.g., SubstClusC on Syn.VSM: 0.520→0.641 oracle, but 0.520→0.576 best-fit)
PPDBClus shows poor Best-Fit performance (0.432 oracle, 0.432 best-fit on Syn.VSM), suggesting method is not universally applicable
No statistical significance testing reported

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Word sense is a meaningful and discrete organizational principle for paraphrases, and paraphrases within a sense are mutually substitutable in most contexts.
supporting_evidence: Example of 'paper' with two sense clusters c1 and c2 (lines 120-130)
Definition of sense inventory as 'a set of sets, {c1, c2, . . . ck}, where each subset contains synonyms of the target t corresponding to one of its senses' (Section 2)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If word senses are not discrete or paraphrases within a sense are not reliably substitutable, then sense-based filtering may introduce noise rather than improve rankings. This would undermine the entire approach.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: B-Cubed F-Score, when applied to sense inventories against human lexsub annotations, is a valid proxy for measuring substitutability fitness for the lexsub task.
supporting_evidence: Section 2: 'A crucial question when evaluating a sense inventory for its fitness for the lexsub task is, how well does it match human judgments about the interchangeability of words?'
B3F metric is applied to Et (overlap between sense inventory and lexsub dataset) to measure agreement between gold sense labels and proposed substitute clusters
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If B3F does not correlate with actual lexsub task performance, then the metric-driven optimization of sense inventories may not improve downstream lexsub results. Section 6 acknowledges this risk: Best-Fit GAP is not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The four views (Context Substitutability, Paraphrase Similarity, WordNet Synsets, Shared Translations) are complementary and each provides independent signal for sense clustering.
supporting_evidence: Multi-view NMF assumes 'the views are complementary, and that each view is likely to cluster the data the same way on its own' (Section 3.1)
Experiments test seven combinations of views (Section 4.2)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If views are not complementary or are highly correlated, multi-view NMF may not provide benefits over single-view clustering. Ablation results (Table 5) show mixed performance across view combinations, suggesting this assumption may not hold uniformly.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: AddCos scores, computed over a large random sample of sentences (1000 sentences per target), provide a reliable estimate of paraphrase substitutability in context.
supporting_evidence: Context Substitutability View uses AddCos scores over 1000 randomly sampled sentences from AGiga
Justification: 'we want to create a method that is scalable and generalizable. Therefore, we choose to measure lexical substitutability using a simple but high-performing vector space model, AddCos'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If 1000 sentences is insufficient to capture the full range of contexts for a target word, or if AddCos scores are biased toward certain types of contexts, the Context Substitutability View may not accurately reflect true substitutability. No sensitivity analysis on sample size is provided.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The PPDB2.0 Score threshold of 2.3 is optimal for balancing coverage and noise in the paraphrase set to be clustered.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.2: 'We chose 2.3 as the threshold score because it gave the best precision and recall when used as a threshold over the CoInCo training data.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the threshold is suboptimal, the resulting sense inventories may have either too much noise (low threshold) or insufficient coverage (high threshold). The choice is tuned on CoInCo training data; generalization to other datasets is unclear.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The number of clusters k (chosen via Silhouette Coefficient maximization over k=2 to 10) is the correct number of senses for each target word.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.2: 'For each target word to be clustered, we try clustering with a range of k between 2 and 10. For each resulting clustering, we calculate the mean Silhouette Coefficient... We choose as the final clustering solution, that clustering which produces the highest Silhouette Coefficient.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the true number of senses for a word falls outside the range [2, 10] or if Silhouette Coefficient does not correlate with true sense granularity, the resulting clusters may be over- or under-segmented. No validation against gold sense inventories (e.g., WordNet) is provided.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The best-fit WSD heuristic (selecting the sense most frequently represented in top-5 ranked substitutes) is a reasonable approximation of the true sense of the target in context.
supporting_evidence: Section 5.4: 'For each target word in context, we choose the 'best-fit' sense to be the sense most frequently represented among the top-5 ranked substitutes by the lexsub ranking model.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the top-5 ranked substitutes do not reliably reflect the true sense (e.g., if the ranking model is biased or if multiple senses are represented equally), the best-fit heuristic will fail. Section 6 acknowledges: 'The simple WSD method fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases; this is an area for improvement.'

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The CoInCo dataset is representative of the types of lexical substitution contexts and sense distributions that the method will encounter in practice.
supporting_evidence: CoInCo is used for both tuning (training set) and evaluation (test set)
327 target words with at least 10 example sentences are selected
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If CoInCo is biased toward certain POS, domains, or sense distributions, the method may not generalize. Section 6 notes: 'The area where our SubstClus inventories are weakest is in improving the lexsub rankings for nouns,' suggesting POS-specific performance variation.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The multi-view NMF hyperparameter λi = 0.01 (regularization weight for all views) is appropriate for balancing view contributions.
supporting_evidence: Supplemental Material A.2: 'In the original paper and in our experiments, we set λi = 0.01 for all i.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If λi is not optimal, the consensus matrix V* may be biased toward certain views. No sensitivity analysis or ablation over λi values is provided.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The extended B-Cubed F-Score with β=0.5 (emphasizing precision over recall) is the appropriate weighting for measuring substitutability.
supporting_evidence: Supplemental Material A.1: 'In our work we use β = 0.5 to emphasize precision over recall in the substitutability score.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If β should be different (e.g., β=1 for equal weighting), the relative rankings of sense inventories may change. No justification for β=0.5 is provided, and no sensitivity analysis is conducted.

argument_focus: Reformulation of lexical substitution as a sense-filtering task rather than a direct ranking task
Integration of multiple complementary views of paraphrase similarity into a unified clustering framework
Validation of B-Cubed F-Score as a metric for sense inventory fitness
Empirical comparison of automatically-generated sense inventories against manually-curated baselines (WordNet+, TWSI) and prior automatic methods (PPDBClus)
Demonstration that oracle sense knowledge yields substantial improvements, but practical WSD approximation yields smaller gains
Identification of POS-specific performance variation (weakness on nouns)
contribution_targets: Novel multi-view clustering method tailored to substitutability (methodological contribution)
SubstClus sense inventories with higher B-Cubed F-Score than existing resources (resource contribution)
Application of sense filtering to improve SOTA lexsub models (practical contribution)
Validation of B-Cubed F-Score as a task-specific metric for sense inventory evaluation (evaluation contribution)
evaluation_targets: Substitutability metric validity: correlation between B-Cubed F-Score and oracle GAP improvements (Section 6)
Sense inventory coverage: number of target words and paraphrases with assigned senses (not explicitly reported)
Clustering quality: Silhouette Coefficient (intrinsic) and B-Cubed F-Score against human annotations (extrinsic) (Section 4.3, Table 2)
Lexsub ranking improvement: oracle GAP and best-fit GAP scores across ranking models (Syn.VSM, AddCos) (Table 5)
Part-of-speech sensitivity: differential performance on nouns vs. other POS (Section 6, Table 5)
Comparison to baselines: WordNet+, TWSI, PPDBClus across B3F and GAP metrics (Table 2, Table 5)
View contribution analysis: ablation study showing impact of each clustering view (Table 5, Figure 1)
Practical applicability: gap between oracle and best-fit performance indicating WSD method effectiveness (Table 5, Section 6)
uncertainty_flags: B-Cubed F-Score superiority does not guarantee lexsub performance improvement; Best-Fit GAP often substantially lower than Oracle GAP
Coverage metrics (number of target words and paraphrases with assigned senses) are not explicitly reported in main results
Performance on nouns is significantly weaker than TWSI, suggesting the method may be POS-dependent
Simple WSD heuristic (best-fit sense selection) has substantial gap from oracle performance (e.g., 0.123 GAP difference for SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM)
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported for GAP improvements
Correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP is stated as 'generally' good but not quantified
Sensitivity to hyperparameters (λi, β, k range, PPDB threshold 2.3, sample size 1000) not explored
Generalization to datasets beyond CoInCo not evaluated
No analysis of failure modes or conditions under which sense filtering breaks down
Multi-view NMF assumption of complementary views not validated; ablation results show mixed performance across view combinations
chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should verify the correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP quantitatively (e.g., Pearson/Spearman correlation coefficient)
Coverage metrics should be extracted and compared across sense inventories to validate the 'wider coverage' claim
POS-specific analysis should be deepened: why does the method fail on nouns? Is it a data issue, a method issue, or a metric issue?
The gap between Oracle and Best-Fit GAP is substantial; reviewers should assess whether the practical applicability claim is justified
Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (especially λi, β, k range) would strengthen claims about method robustness
Statistical significance testing should be applied to all GAP comparisons
The assumption that the four views are complementary should be validated (e.g., via correlation analysis or information-theoretic measures)
Generalization to other lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007) should be evaluated to assess external validity
The simple WSD heuristic should be compared to more sophisticated WSD methods to establish a performance ceiling

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper proposes a multi-view clustering method (SubstClus) to automatically generate word sense inventories optimized for lexical substitution (lexsub), and demonstrates that these inventories can filter and improve rankings from vector-based lexsub models. The logical structure follows a clear progression: (1) motivation that SOTA lexsub models ignore sense, (2) definition of substitutability via B-Cubed F-Score, (3) multi-view NMF method incorporating four complementary views, (4) clustering experiments on CoInCo, (5) oracle and practical sense-filtering experiments. The core argument chain is coherent but exhibits critical gaps between metric validity (B3F superiority) and practical task performance (Best-Fit GAP substantially lower than Oracle GAP). The paper's reasoning strengthens in the methodological design (multi-view integration is well-motivated) but weakens in the practical applicability section, where the simple WSD heuristic fails to approximate oracle performance, particularly on nouns. The paper acknowledges but does not resolve this gap, limiting the strength of its practical contribution claim.
logical_argument_graph: SOTA lexsub models ignore word sense (C1 premise) → sense filtering can improve rankings (C1 conclusion)
Substitutability is a measurable property of sense inventories (A1 assumption) → B-Cubed F-Score is a valid metric for measuring it (C3 claim)
Four views are complementary and encode substitutability signals (A3 assumption) → multi-view NMF produces more substitutable clusters than single-view methods (C2 claim)
Automatically-generated inventories exceed WordNet/TWSI in B3F (C2 evidence) → they exceed them in practical lexsub performance (C5 claim, weakly supported)
Oracle experiment shows sense filtering improves GAP (C5 evidence) → simple WSD approximates oracle performance (C4 claim, contradicted by results)
Best-Fit GAP is substantially lower than Oracle GAP (Section 6 results) → practical applicability is limited (implicit concern, not explicitly addressed)
POS-specific performance variation observed (Section 6) → method effectiveness is context-dependent (implicit finding, not integrated into main claims)

identified_claims.claim_label: SOTA lexsub models ignore sense but can be improved by filtering
identified_claims.claim_text: Current state-of-the-art lexical substitution models ignore word sense, instead relying on powerful vector and embedded word representations to find good substitutes. These models can be improved by integrating word sense inventories to filter substitutes from the correct sense to the top of the rankings.
evidence: Introduction explicitly contrasts early two-step (sense→substitutes) approaches with current SOTA (direct ranking without sense)
Hypothesis stated at lines 140-150: high-coverage, substitutable sense inventory can improve SOTA models
Oracle GAP results (Table 5) show improvements across all inventories when sense is known

identified_claims.claim_label: B-Cubed F-Score is valid metric for sense inventory fitness for lexsub

evidence: Section 2: B3F proposed as metric for comparing automatically-generated inventories against human-generated substitutability judgments
Section 6: 'our substitutability metric is generally a good indicator of the potential for a sense inventory to improve lexsub rankings'
Table 2 and Table 5 show general alignment between B3F rankings and Oracle GAP rankings

strengths.title: Well-motivated problem reformulation
strengths.description: The paper effectively reframes lexical substitution as a sense-filtering task, providing clear motivation for why sense inventories matter despite SOTA models ignoring sense. The 'paper' example (Table 1) effectively illustrates the problem.
evidence: Introduction clearly contrasts early two-step approaches with current SOTA
Hypothesis is explicit and testable
Table 1 provides concrete example of sense-dependent substitutability

strengths.title: Methodologically sound multi-view integration
strengths.description: The four views (Context Substitutability, Paraphrase Similarity, WordNet Synsets, Shared Translations) are well-chosen and theoretically motivated. Each view encodes a different signal relevant to substitutability, and the multi-view NMF framework is appropriate for combining them.
evidence: Section 3 provides clear rationale for each view
Views are complementary in principle (context, paraphrase strength, structured knowledge, cross-lingual signal)
Multi-view NMF is established technique adapted appropriately for this task

strengths.title: Comprehensive experimental design with oracle baseline
strengths.description: The oracle experiment (Section 5.4) is well-designed to establish an upper bound on sense-filtering improvements. This allows separation of method limitations from WSD limitations, providing clear diagnostic value.
evidence: Oracle experiment isolates the effect of sense filtering from WSD accuracy
Table 4 provides concrete example showing oracle improvement mechanism
Comparison of Oracle vs Best-Fit GAP clearly shows practical gap

strengths.title: Honest reporting of limitations and failure cases
strengths.description: The paper explicitly acknowledges POS-specific performance variation (Section 6), noting that the method is weakest on nouns and that TWSI outperforms SubstClus on noun-only evaluation. This transparency strengthens credibility.
evidence: Section 6: 'The area where our SubstClus inventories are weakest is in improving the lexsub rankings for nouns'
Section 6: 'The simple WSD method fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases; this is an area for improvement'
Table 5 shows noun-only results separately, revealing performance degradation

strengths.title: Clear metric definition and justification
strengths.description: B-Cubed F-Score is formally defined (Section 2.1, Supplemental A.1) with clear explanation of why it is appropriate for measuring substitutability. The extended version allowing multiple cluster membership is well-motivated.
evidence: Section 2.1 provides full definition of B3F with precision/recall components
Supplemental A.1 explains extended B3F and β=0.5 choice
Metric is applied consistently across all sense inventories

strengths.title: Reproducible experimental setup
strengths.description: The paper provides sufficient detail for reproduction: data splits (60/40 train/test), hyperparameter choices (k range 2-10, PPDB threshold 2.3, λi=0.01), and implementation details (AddCos parameters, word2vec settings in Supplemental A.3).
evidence: Section 4.1: CoInCo split and target word selection clearly specified
Section 4.2: PPDB threshold justification and k selection method described
Supplemental A.2-A.3: Multi-view NMF and AddCos implementation details provided

concerns.title: Substantial gap between oracle and practical performance not adequately addressed
concerns.description: The Best-Fit GAP scores are substantially lower than Oracle GAP scores (e.g., SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM: 0.675 oracle vs 0.552 best-fit, an 18% relative loss). This undermines the practical applicability claim, yet the paper does not deeply analyze why or propose solutions.
evidence: Table 5 shows consistent oracle-to-best-fit degradation across all inventories
SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM: 0.675→0.552 (0.123 absolute loss)
SubstClusCPWT on AddCos: 0.671→0.542 (0.129 absolute loss)
Section 6 acknowledges: 'The simple WSD method fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases' but offers no analysis
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add failure mode analysis: categorize cases where best-fit WSD fails (e.g., multiple senses equally represented in top-5, rare senses, POS-specific issues). Propose more sophisticated WSD methods (e.g., using context embeddings, comparing to existing WSD systems) and evaluate their performance. Quantify the oracle-to-best-fit gap as a function of sense inventory properties.

concerns.title: B-Cubed F-Score correlation with Oracle GAP not quantified
concerns.description: The paper claims B3F is 'generally a good indicator' of Oracle GAP potential (Section 6) but provides no correlation coefficient (Pearson, Spearman, or other). This weakens the validation of the metric as a task-specific measure.
evidence: Section 6: 'we find that our substitutability metric is generally a good indicator' (qualitative, not quantitative)
No correlation analysis provided between Table 2 B3F scores and Table 5 Oracle GAP scores
Section 6 also states: 'Best-Fit GAP scores are not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP scores', indicating metric limitations
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients between B3F scores (Table 2) and Oracle GAP scores (Table 5) for all sense inventories. Report correlation with confidence intervals. If correlation is weak, discuss implications for using B3F as an optimization target.

concerns.title: Coverage metrics claimed but not reported
concerns.description: The abstract claims sense inventories have 'wider coverage' than existing inventories, but coverage metrics are not explicitly reported in the main results. Only 'Avg CoInCo Overlap' is shown in Table 2, which is not the same as overall coverage.
evidence: Abstract: 'wider coverage than existing sense inventories'
Table 2 shows 'Avg CoInCo Overlap' (5.5-16.6 words per target) but not total coverage
No reporting of: total number of unique paraphrases covered, percentage of PPDB covered, or coverage by POS
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report coverage metrics explicitly: (1) total number of unique paraphrases in each sense inventory, (2) percentage of PPDB paraphrases covered, (3) coverage by POS. Compare to WordNet+, TWSI, and PPDBClus. Clarify whether 'wider coverage' refers to number of target words, number of paraphrases per target, or both.

concerns.title: Multi-view complementarity assumption not validated
concerns.description: The paper assumes the four views are complementary (Section 3.1), but provides no validation of this assumption. Ablation results (Table 5) show mixed performance across view combinations, suggesting views may not be equally complementary.
evidence: Section 3.1: 'Multi-view NMF assumes that the views are complementary'
Table 5 ablation results show inconsistent performance: SubstClusCP (0.681) outperforms SubstClusCPWT (0.675) on Syn.VSM unfiltered
SubstClusP (0.692) outperforms all multi-view combinations on Syn.VSM unfiltered
No analysis of view correlation or information-theoretic redundancy
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute pairwise correlations between the four view matrices (XS, XP, XW, XF) to assess redundancy. Perform information-theoretic analysis (e.g., mutual information) to quantify complementarity. Analyze why single-view SubstClusP sometimes outperforms multi-view combinations. Consider view weighting (λi) as a hyperparameter to optimize.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter sensitivity not explored
concerns.description: Multiple hyperparameters are fixed without sensitivity analysis: PPDB threshold (2.3), k range (2-10), λi (0.01), β (0.5), sample size for AddCos (1000 sentences). No ablation or sensitivity study is provided.
evidence: Section 4.2: PPDB threshold 2.3 chosen because 'it gave the best precision and recall when used as a threshold over the CoInCo training data' (tuned on training set only)
Section 4.2: k range 2-10 chosen arbitrarily; no justification for upper bound
Supplemental A.2: λi=0.01 set 'in the original paper and in our experiments' (not tuned)
Supplemental A.1: β=0.5 chosen 'to emphasize precision over recall' (no justification or sensitivity analysis)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct sensitivity analysis for: (1) PPDB threshold (test 2.0, 2.3, 2.5, 3.0), (2) k range (test upper bounds 5, 10, 15), (3) λi values (test 0.001, 0.01, 0.1), (4) β values (test 0.25, 0.5, 1.0). Report impact on B3F and Oracle GAP. Identify which hyperparameters have largest effect.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing reported
concerns.description: All GAP improvements are reported as point estimates without confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. It is unclear whether improvements are statistically significant or within noise margins.
evidence: Table 5 reports point estimates only (e.g., 0.675, 0.552) with no error bars or confidence intervals
No mention of statistical testing (t-tests, bootstrap, permutation tests)
Some improvements are small (e.g., SubstClusC on Syn.VSM: 0.520→0.641 oracle, but 0.520→0.576 best-fit is only 0.056 improvement)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute 95% confidence intervals for all GAP scores using bootstrap resampling (resample sentences with replacement). Perform paired t-tests comparing each sense inventory to baselines. Report p-values and effect sizes. Identify which improvements are statistically significant at p<0.05.

concerns.title: POS-specific performance variation not deeply analyzed
concerns.description: The paper identifies that the method is weakest on nouns (Section 6, Table 5) but does not analyze why or propose POS-specific solutions. This limits the generalizability claim.
evidence: Section 6: 'The area where our SubstClus inventories are weakest is in improving the lexsub rankings for nouns'
Table 5 shows noun-only Oracle GAP for SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM (0.669) is lower than all-words (0.675)
TWSI significantly outperforms SubstClus on nouns (0.756 vs 0.669 oracle on Syn.VSM)
No analysis of why nouns are problematic or how to address it
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze noun-specific failure modes: (1) compare sense granularity for nouns vs other POS, (2) examine whether noun senses are more fine-grained or ambiguous, (3) test whether TWSI's crowdsourced approach is better for nouns, (4) propose POS-specific view weighting or clustering parameters. Consider developing separate inventories for different POS.

concerns.title: Generalization to other lexsub datasets not evaluated
concerns.description: The method is evaluated only on CoInCo (327 target words). Generalization to other lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007, SemEval-2015) is not tested, limiting external validity claims.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'We draw the target words for our clustering experiment from the Concepts In Context (CoInCo) dataset'
Section 5.1: 'We use the test portion of the CoInCo subset defined in Section 4.1'
No mention of evaluation on SemEval-2007 or other standard lexsub benchmarks
Related work (Section 7) mentions SemEval-2007 but does not evaluate on it
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate SubstClus on SemEval-2007 Lexical Substitution task and other available lexsub datasets. Compare Oracle and Best-Fit GAP to baselines. Analyze whether performance patterns (POS-specific variation, oracle-to-best-fit gap) generalize across datasets. Discuss dataset-specific differences.

concerns.title: Simple WSD heuristic not compared to existing WSD methods
concerns.description: The best-fit WSD method (top-5 frequency) is ad-hoc and not compared to existing WSD systems. This makes it unclear whether the poor practical performance is due to the method or to fundamental limitations of sense filtering.
evidence: Section 5.4: best-fit heuristic is 'choose the sense most frequently represented among the top-5 ranked substitutes'
No comparison to existing WSD methods (e.g., Lesk algorithm, supervised WSD classifiers, contextualized embeddings)
Section 6 acknowledges failure but does not propose alternatives
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compare best-fit WSD to: (1) Lesk algorithm using sense inventory definitions, (2) supervised WSD classifier trained on SemCor, (3) contextualized embeddings (e.g., BERT) for sense selection. Evaluate each method's Oracle-to-Best-Fit gap. Identify which WSD approach best approximates oracle performance.

concerns.title: Novelty of multi-view clustering approach is incremental
concerns.description: The paper applies multi-view NMF (Liu et al., 2013) to a new task (lexsub sense clustering) with new views. While the application is novel, the core algorithmic contribution is limited. The main novelty is in the problem reformulation and view engineering.
evidence: Multi-view NMF is established technique from Liu et al. (2013)
Four views are relatively straightforward applications of existing ideas (AddCos for context, PPDB scores for paraphrase similarity, WordNet for structure, translations for cross-lingual signal)
No algorithmic innovations to multi-view NMF itself
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the novelty contribution: is it primarily the problem reformulation (lexsub as sense filtering), the view engineering, or the empirical validation? Consider whether algorithmic innovations (e.g., view weighting, adaptive λi, hierarchical clustering) would strengthen the contribution.

concerns.title: Sparse precedent for substitutability-focused sense clustering
concerns.description: The paper claims to be the first to optimize sense clustering specifically for substitutability (rather than general paraphrase similarity). This is a novel angle, but the paper does not sufficiently explore related work in substitutability metrics or sense induction.
evidence: Related work (Section 7) focuses on lexsub models and paraphrase clustering, not substitutability-focused sense induction
TWSI (Biemann, 2013) is mentioned as crowdsourced with 'substitutability in mind', but the paper does not deeply compare approaches
No discussion of other substitutability metrics or sense induction methods
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Expand related work to include: (1) other substitutability metrics (e.g., from paraphrase evaluation), (2) sense induction methods optimized for specific tasks, (3) crowdsourced sense inventories (TWSI, OntoNotes). Clarify what is novel about the substitutability-focused approach.

comparable_works.relevance: Directly comparable prior work on clustering PPDB paraphrases by sense using spectral clustering
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Both cluster PPDB paraphrases by sense, but Cocos & Callison-Burch use spectral clustering with PPDB2.0 Score, while this paper uses multi-view NMF with four views. This paper claims higher substitutability (B3F) and better lexsub performance.

comparable_works.relevance: Crowdsourced sense inventory developed with substitutability in mind; serves as baseline
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: TWSI is manually curated for nouns only; this paper's SubstClus is automatically generated for all POS. TWSI outperforms SubstClus on nouns (Table 5), suggesting crowdsourcing may be superior for certain POS.

comparable_works.relevance: Lexsub ranking model used as baseline and for computing Context Substitutability view
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: AddCos is a vector-space lexsub model that ignores sense; this paper uses AddCos scores to construct a sense-aware view for clustering. The paper demonstrates that sense filtering can improve AddCos rankings.

comparable_works.relevance: Syntactic vector space lexsub model used as baseline ranking model
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Syn.VSM is another sense-agnostic lexsub model; this paper shows sense filtering improves its rankings. Syn.VSM is used as the primary baseline for oracle and best-fit experiments.

comparable_works.relevance: Core algorithmic technique used for clustering
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This paper applies multi-view NMF (established technique) to a new task (lexsub sense clustering) with novel views. No algorithmic innovations to multi-view NMF itself.

comparable_works.relevance: Clustering evaluation metric adapted for measuring substitutability
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This paper applies extended B-Cubed F-Score (established metric) to a new task (sense inventory evaluation for lexsub). The metric is well-motivated but its correlation with task performance is not quantified.

uncertainty_flags: B-Cubed F-Score superiority does not guarantee lexsub performance improvement; Best-Fit GAP often substantially lower than Oracle GAP, indicating metric-task misalignment
Coverage metrics ('wider coverage' claim in abstract) are not explicitly reported; only CoInCo overlap is shown
Performance on nouns is significantly weaker than TWSI, suggesting method may be POS-dependent and not universally applicable
Simple WSD heuristic (best-fit sense selection) has substantial gap from oracle performance (18% relative loss on average), limiting practical applicability
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported for GAP improvements; unclear if improvements are statistically significant
Correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP is stated as 'generally' good but not quantified; no correlation coefficient provided
Sensitivity to hyperparameters (λi, β, k range, PPDB threshold 2.3, sample size 1000) not explored; unclear how robust method is to parameter choices
Generalization to datasets beyond CoInCo not evaluated; external validity unclear
No analysis of failure modes or conditions under which sense filtering breaks down; best-fit WSD method sometimes degrades performance
Multi-view NMF assumption of complementary views not validated; ablation results show mixed performance across view combinations, suggesting views may be redundant
alternative_interpretations: The oracle-to-best-fit GAP gap could reflect not a limitation of sense filtering, but rather the difficulty of the WSD task itself. A more sophisticated WSD method might better approximate oracle performance, suggesting the problem is WSD accuracy rather than sense filtering validity.

The POS-specific performance variation (weakness on nouns) could be due to data characteristics (CoInCo may have fewer noun examples or noisier annotations) rather than method limitations. Evaluation on balanced POS datasets might show different results.

B-Cubed F-Score may be a valid metric for sense inventory quality in general, but not specifically for the lexsub task. The metric optimizes for precision/recall of sense clustering, which may not align with lexsub ranking quality. Alternative metrics (e.g., task-specific metrics) might show stronger correlation.

The multi-view NMF approach may not be necessary; single-view clustering (SubstClusP) sometimes outperforms multi-view combinations (Table 5), suggesting that paraphrase similarity alone may be sufficient and other views add noise.

The sense filtering approach may be fundamentally limited by the assumption that sense is discrete and that paraphrases within a sense are mutually substitutable. In reality, substitutability may be context-dependent and continuous, making discrete sense clusters suboptimal.
transparency_notes: The paper is generally transparent about limitations: POS-specific performance variation is acknowledged, oracle-to-best-fit gap is reported, and failure of simple WSD method is mentioned. However, these limitations are not deeply analyzed or addressed.

The paper does not discuss potential confounds: improvements in oracle GAP could be due to re-ranking effects rather than sense filtering per se. Ablation studies isolating the effect of sense filtering from other factors would strengthen claims.
The paper does not discuss computational complexity: multi-view NMF requires factorizing four matrices for each target word; scalability to large paraphrase databases is unclear.

The paper does not discuss the choice of CoInCo as the evaluation dataset: CoInCo may have specific characteristics (e.g., domain, sense distribution, annotation quality) that affect generalizability. Evaluation on multiple datasets would strengthen claims.

The paper does not discuss the relationship between sense inventory size and performance: larger inventories (PPDBClus) have lower B3F but sometimes better Best-Fit GAP, suggesting a trade-off between coverage and precision that is not explored.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The substitutability-focused sense clustering approach is novel and lacks close analogs in the retrieved literature. However, novelty does not guarantee validity or practical impact. The oracle-to-best-fit gap and POS-specific performance variation suggest the approach has limitations that are not fully addressed.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If a more sophisticated WSD method (e.g., using contextualized embeddings) could better approximate oracle performance, the practical applicability of sense filtering would be strengthened.
If the method were evaluated on multiple lexsub datasets (SemEval-2007, SemEval-2015) and showed consistent improvements, external validity would be established.
If POS-specific performance variation were analyzed and addressed (e.g., with POS-specific view weighting or clustering parameters), the method's generalizability would improve.
If the correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP were quantified and shown to be strong (r > 0.8), the metric would be validated as a task-specific measure.
If hyperparameter sensitivity analysis showed the method is robust to parameter choices, confidence in the approach would increase.
If the multi-view complementarity assumption were validated (e.g., via correlation analysis), the necessity of the multi-view approach would be established.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper applies multi-view NMF (established technique) to a new task (lexsub sense clustering) with novel views. The core algorithmic contribution is limited, but the problem reformulation (lexsub as sense filtering) and view engineering are novel. The empirical validation is thorough but limited to one dataset.
evidence: Multi-view NMF is from Liu et al. (2013); no algorithmic innovations
Four views are straightforward applications of existing ideas (AddCos, PPDB scores, WordNet, translations)
Problem reformulation (lexsub as sense filtering) is novel and well-motivated
Empirical validation is limited to CoInCo; generalization not tested
uncertainty_flags: Unclear whether the novelty is primarily in problem reformulation or in the method itself
The paper does not clearly position its novelty relative to prior work on sense induction and substitutability metrics

novelty_lenses.verdict: Limited disruptive potential due to practical limitations
novelty_lenses.rationale: While the problem reformulation is novel, the practical impact is limited by the oracle-to-best-fit gap, POS-specific performance variation, and lack of generalization to other datasets. The method does not substantially outperform simpler baselines (e.g., TWSI on nouns), and the simple WSD heuristic fails in many cases.
evidence: Best-Fit GAP is substantially lower than Oracle GAP (18% relative loss), limiting practical applicability
TWSI outperforms SubstClus on nouns, suggesting crowdsourcing may be superior
Method is evaluated only on CoInCo; generalization unclear
Simple WSD method fails on nouns; no alternative WSD methods tested
uncertainty_flags: More sophisticated WSD methods might better approximate oracle performance, increasing practical impact
Evaluation on other datasets might show different results and higher practical impact

novelty_lenses.verdict: Moderate resource contribution with limited practical utility
novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper creates SubstClus sense inventories for 327 target words from CoInCo. These inventories have higher B3F than WordNet and TWSI, but practical lexsub improvements are inconsistent. The resource is limited in scope (only 327 words) and POS-specific performance variation suggests it may not be universally useful.
evidence: SubstClus inventories cover 327 target words from CoInCo
B3F scores are higher than WordNet+ and TWSI (Table 2)
Best-Fit GAP improvements are inconsistent and sometimes negative
TWSI outperforms SubstClus on nouns, limiting utility for noun substitution
uncertainty_flags: Unclear whether SubstClus inventories will be released and made available to the community
Coverage is limited to 327 words; scalability to full PPDB is unclear

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper presents a well-motivated problem reformulation and a methodologically sound approach with comprehensive experimental design. However, significant concerns limit confidence: (1) the oracle-to-best-fit gap substantially undermines practical applicability claims, (2) POS-specific performance variation suggests limited generalizability, (3) key metrics (B3F-Oracle GAP correlation) are not quantified, (4) generalization to other datasets is not tested, (5) hyperparameter sensitivity is not explored. The paper makes a solid methodological contribution but falls short of demonstrating strong practical impact. The honest reporting of limitations increases credibility, but the lack of deep analysis of failure modes and proposed solutions decreases confidence in the overall contribution. The novelty is moderate (problem reformulation + view engineering) but not disruptive. Overall, this is a competent methodological paper with incremental contributions and acknowledged limitations, suitable for publication with revisions addressing the major concerns.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper proposes a multi-view NMF clustering method to automatically generate sense inventories optimized for lexical substitution (lexsub), with the goal of filtering and improving rankings from vector-based lexsub models. The core argument is that current SOTA lexsub models ignore word sense but can be improved by filtering substitutes through high-quality sense inventories. The method combines four complementary views (Context Substitutability, Paraphrase Similarity, WordNet Synsets, Shared Translations) and is evaluated on the CoInCo dataset using B-Cubed F-Score as a substitutability metric and GAP as a lexsub performance metric. The paper demonstrates oracle improvements but acknowledges substantial gaps between oracle and practical (best-fit) performance. Key methodological strengths include the multi-view approach and task-specific metric design; key concerns include unvalidated assumptions about view complementarity, limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, POS-dependent performance variation, and the gap between metric-level and task-level improvements.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: Current SOTA lexsub models rely on vector similarity and ignore explicit sense disambiguation (lines 100-110).
Premise 2: Word sense is a meaningful organizational principle for paraphrases; paraphrases within a sense are mutually substitutable (Introduction, Section 2).
Premise 3: High-coverage, substitutable sense inventories can be used as filters to improve lexsub rankings (lines 140-150).
Conclusion 1 (C1): Sense filtering is a viable approach to improve SOTA lexsub models.

Premise 4: Multi-view clustering can incorporate complementary signals (context substitutability, paraphrase similarity, WordNet structure, foreign translations) to generate substitutable sense clusters (Section 3).
Premise 5: B-Cubed F-Score measures agreement between sense inventories and human lexsub annotations, serving as a proxy for substitutability fitness (Section 2.1).
Conclusion 2 (C2): Multi-view clustering produces more substitutable sense clusters than existing inventories (measured by B3F).
Premise 6: Oracle experiments show that perfect sense knowledge yields substantial GAP improvements (Table 5).
Premise 7: A simple WSD heuristic (best-fit sense selection from top-5 ranked substitutes) approximates oracle performance (Section 5.4).
Conclusion 3 (C4): Simple WSD can approximate oracle performance in practical settings.
Premise 8: Best-Fit GAP scores are substantially lower than Oracle GAP scores, indicating WSD method limitations (Table 5, Section 6).
Caveat 1: The gap between oracle and best-fit performance is substantial and POS-dependent (Section 6).
Caveat 2: B3F superiority does not guarantee lexsub task improvement; correlation is 'generally' good but unquantified (Section 6).
Caveat 3: Multi-view NMF assumes view complementarity, but ablation results show mixed performance (Table 5).

identified_claims.claim_label: SOTA lexsub models ignore sense but can be improved by filtering
identified_claims.claim_text: Current state-of-the-art lexical substitution models ignore word sense, instead relying on powerful vector and embedded word representations to find good substitutes. These models can be improved by integrating word sense inventories to filter substitutes from the correct sense to the top of the rankings.
evidence: Lines 100-110: 'But current state-of-the-art lexical substitution systems ignore the sense disambiguation step altogether, instead relying on vector space models to find substitutes that are semantically similar to the target, and contextually appropriate.'

Lines 140-150: 'Our hypothesis is that a high-coverage, substitutable sense inventory – one in which words belonging to a single sense are mutually substitutable in most contexts – can be used in combination with a word-based lexsub model to improve the quality of proposed substitutes.'
Table 4: Example showing GAP improvement from 0.47 to 0.78 via sense filtering for target 'year'.
uncertainty_flags: No explicit evidence that contextualized embeddings (e.g., BERT-style models) cannot implicitly capture sense distinctions.
Claim assumes sense filtering is the primary mechanism; alternative explanations (e.g., re-ranking bias, candidate set effects) not ruled out.
Oracle experiment assumes perfect sense knowledge; practical applicability limited by WSD method quality.

identified_claims.claim_label: Multi-view clustering produces more substitutable sense clusters
identified_claims.claim_text: Multi-view clustering incorporating context substitutability, paraphrase similarity, WordNet structure, and foreign translations produces sense clusters that are more substitutable and have wider coverage than existing sense inventories (WordNet+, PPDBClus, TWSI).
evidence: Section 4.3: 'all multi-view inventories and the SubstClusP single-view inventory are more substitutable than WordNet and TWSI in terms of B-Cubed F-Score.'
Table 2: B3F0.5 scores show SubstClus inventories (not explicitly reported in main table) vs. WordNet+ (0.841), TWSI (0.842), PPDBClus (0.736).
Table 5: Oracle GAP scores for SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM (0.675) and AddCos (0.671) exceed or match baselines.
uncertainty_flags: B3F superiority does not directly translate to lexsub performance improvement; Best-Fit GAP often substantially lower than Oracle GAP.
Coverage metrics ('wider coverage') not explicitly quantified in main results; claim lacks numerical support.
Performance on nouns significantly weaker than TWSI (Section 6), suggesting POS-dependent effectiveness.
Ablation results (Table 5) show mixed performance across view combinations, questioning assumption of complementarity.

identified_claims.claim_label: B-Cubed F-Score is valid metric for sense inventory fitness for lexsub
identified_claims.claim_text: B-Cubed F-Score is a valid metric for measuring sense inventory fitness for the lexical substitution task, as it correlates with oracle GAP improvements.
evidence: Section 2: 'We propose a cluster quality metric, B-Cubed F-Score (Amigó et al., 2009), as a way of comparing an automatically-generated sense inventory against a human-generated set of substitutability judgements.'

Section 6: 'Comparing the B-Cubed F-Score for the sense inventories to the Oracle GAP scores, we find that our substitutability metric is generally a good indicator of the potential for a sense inventory to improve lexsub rankings.'
uncertainty_flags: Correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP stated as 'generally' good but not quantified (no Pearson/Spearman coefficient provided).
Section 6 explicitly states: 'The Best-Fit GAP scores are not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP scores, however, indicating that our simple WSD method may introduce bias.'
B3F uses β=0.5 to emphasize precision; sensitivity to β parameter choice not explored.
Metric is evaluated only on CoInCo; generalization to other lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007) not tested.

identified_claims.claim_label: Simple WSD method approximates oracle performance
identified_claims.claim_text: A simple word sense disambiguation method (best-fit sense selection based on top-5 ranked substitutes) can approximate oracle performance in practical sense filtering for lexical substitution.
evidence: Section 5.4: 'For each target word in context, we choose the 'best-fit' sense to be the sense most frequently represented among the top-5 ranked substitutes by the lexsub ranking model.'
Section 6: 'in most cases, all sense inventories except PPDBClus can improve the GAP score when a simple WSD method is applied (Best-Fit GAP).'
uncertainty_flags: Gap between Oracle and Best-Fit GAP is substantial: SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM shows 0.675 oracle vs 0.552 best-fit (0.123 difference, 18% relative gap).
Section 6 acknowledges: 'The simple WSD method fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases; this is an area for improvement.'
Method fails specifically on nouns (Section 6), indicating POS-dependent performance.
No analysis of failure modes, conditions under which best-fit breaks down, or comparison to more sophisticated WSD methods.
Heuristic choice (top-5 frequency) lacks justification; no sensitivity analysis on window size.

identified_claims.claim_label: Sense filtering improves lexsub rankings across models
identified_claims.claim_text: Sense filtering using automatically-generated sense inventories can significantly improve lexical substitution rankings generated by existing vector- and embedding-based models (Syn.VSM, AddCos).
evidence: Table 5: Oracle GAP improvements across all sense inventories for both Syn.VSM and AddCos.
Section 6: 'All baseline and clustered sense inventories can improve the GAP score of the Syn.VSM and AddCos ranking models when used as a filter, based on Oracle GAP scores.'
Table 4: Example showing GAP improvement from 0.47 to 0.78 for target 'year'.
uncertainty_flags: Oracle experiment assumes perfect sense knowledge; practical Best-Fit improvements are much smaller and inconsistent.
Improvement magnitude varies widely: SubstClusC on Syn.VSM shows 0.520→0.641 oracle (0.121 improvement) but 0.520→0.576 best-fit (0.056 improvement, 54% reduction).
PPDBClus shows poor Best-Fit performance (0.432 oracle, 0.432 best-fit on Syn.VSM), suggesting method is not universally applicable.
No statistical significance testing reported; unclear if improvements are statistically significant.

Unfiltered GAP scores for SubstClus inventories sometimes lower than baselines (e.g., SubstClusC: 0.520 vs WordNet+ 0.655 on Syn.VSM), suggesting method may degrade performance without oracle sense knowledge.

strengths.title: Novel multi-view clustering approach tailored to substitutability
strengths.description: The paper introduces a principled multi-view NMF method that incorporates four complementary signals (context substitutability, paraphrase similarity, WordNet structure, foreign translations) specifically designed for the lexsub task. This is a methodologically sound combination that goes beyond prior single-view approaches (e.g., PPDBClus).
evidence: Section 3: Clear motivation for each view and how it relates to substitutability.
Section 3.1.1-3.1.4: Detailed technical descriptions of each view construction.
Table 5: Ablation study showing performance of different view combinations.

strengths.title: Task-specific metric design (B-Cubed F-Score for substitutability)
strengths.description: The paper proposes B-Cubed F-Score as a task-specific metric for evaluating sense inventory fitness for lexsub, moving beyond generic clustering metrics. This is a principled choice that directly measures agreement with human substitutability judgments.
evidence: Section 2.1: Clear definition of B3F application to lexsub annotations.
Supplemental Material A.1: Detailed mathematical formulation.
Section 6: Validation that B3F correlates with oracle GAP improvements.

strengths.title: Comprehensive empirical evaluation with oracle and practical experiments
strengths.description: The paper conducts both oracle experiments (upper bound) and practical experiments (best-fit WSD), providing a clear picture of the method's potential and limitations. This two-stage evaluation is methodologically sound and transparent.
evidence: Section 5.3-5.4: Clear description of oracle and best-fit experimental setup.
Table 5: Comprehensive results across multiple sense inventories and ranking models.
Section 6: Honest acknowledgment of gap between oracle and best-fit performance.

strengths.title: Clear problem reformulation and motivation
strengths.description: The paper effectively reframes lexsub as a sense-filtering task, providing clear motivation (Table 1 example) for why sense inventories matter. The introduction clearly articulates the hypothesis and expected benefits.
evidence: Table 1: Concrete example showing how sense clusters improve substitutability.
Lines 100-150: Clear articulation of the problem and hypothesis.
Table 4: Concrete example of sense filtering improving GAP.

strengths.title: Honest reporting of limitations and failure modes
strengths.description: The paper transparently reports POS-specific performance variation (weakness on nouns), the gap between oracle and best-fit performance, and acknowledges that the simple WSD method 'fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases.' This transparency is valuable for downstream research.
evidence: Section 6: 'The area where our SubstClus inventories are weakest is in improving the lexsub rankings for nouns.'
Section 6: 'The simple WSD method fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases; this is an area for improvement.'
Table 5: Explicit reporting of both oracle and best-fit GAP scores.

strengths.title: Reproducible experimental setup with clear data splits
strengths.description: The paper provides clear details on data splits (60% train, 40% test), hyperparameter choices (k range 2-10, PPDB threshold 2.3, λi=0.01), and evaluation metrics. This enables reproducibility.
evidence: Section 4.1: Clear description of CoInCo data split.
Section 4.2: Explicit hyperparameter choices and justification for PPDB threshold.
Supplemental Material A.2-A.3: Detailed implementation details for multi-view NMF and AddCos.

concerns.title: Unvalidated assumption of view complementarity
concerns.description: The multi-view NMF method assumes that the four views are complementary and each provides independent signal for sense clustering. However, this assumption is not validated. Ablation results (Table 5) show mixed performance across view combinations, with some single-view inventories (e.g., SubstClusP) outperforming multi-view combinations on certain metrics.
evidence: Section 3.1: 'Multi-view NMF assumes that the views are complementary, and that each view is likely to cluster the data the same way on its own.'
Table 5: SubstClusP (single view) shows Oracle GAP of 0.692 on Syn.VSM, while SubstClusCPWT (all views) shows 0.675. On AddCos, SubstClusP shows 0.686 vs SubstClusCPWT 0.671.
No correlation analysis or information-theoretic measures provided to validate view independence.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct correlation analysis between views (e.g., Pearson correlation of paraphrase-paraphrase matrices, mutual information between view-based clusterings). Report whether views are truly independent or if some are redundant. Investigate why single-view clustering sometimes outperforms multi-view combinations.

concerns.title: Unquantified correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP
concerns.description: The paper claims that B3F is 'generally a good indicator' of oracle GAP potential (Section 6), but provides no quantitative correlation coefficient (Pearson/Spearman). The word 'generally' is vague and undermines the validity claim for the metric.
evidence: Section 6: 'Comparing the B-Cubed F-Score for the sense inventories to the Oracle GAP scores, we find that our substitutability metric is generally a good indicator of the potential for a sense inventory to improve lexsub rankings.'
No correlation coefficient provided; no scatter plot or statistical test.

Section 6 also states: 'The Best-Fit GAP scores are not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP scores, however, indicating that our simple WSD method may introduce bias.' This suggests even oracle-level correlation may be imperfect.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute and report Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients between B3F scores and Oracle GAP scores across all sense inventories and target words. Provide a scatter plot with regression line. If correlation is moderate or weak, revise the claim about metric validity.

concerns.title: Substantial gap between oracle and best-fit performance not adequately addressed
concerns.description: The gap between oracle and best-fit GAP is substantial (e.g., SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM: 0.675 oracle vs 0.552 best-fit, an 18% relative gap). This undermines the practical applicability claim. The paper acknowledges the gap but does not provide sufficient analysis of failure modes or conditions under which the simple WSD heuristic breaks down.
evidence: Table 5: Consistent large gaps between oracle and best-fit across all inventories and models.
Section 6: 'The simple WSD method fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases; this is an area for improvement.' No analysis of when/why it fails.
Section 5.4: The best-fit heuristic (top-5 frequency) is simple and heuristic; no justification for why this particular heuristic should work.
No comparison to more sophisticated WSD methods (e.g., Lesk algorithm, neural WSD models) to establish a performance ceiling.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct error analysis: (1) For instances where best-fit fails, analyze what went wrong (e.g., was the correct sense not in top-5? Was it tied with other senses?). (2) Compare the simple WSD heuristic to more sophisticated WSD methods (e.g., Lesk, neural models) to establish a performance ceiling. (3) Investigate whether the gap is due to the WSD method or the sense inventory quality.

concerns.title: POS-dependent performance variation not adequately explained
concerns.description: The paper reports that SubstClus inventories are 'weakest in improving the lexsub rankings for nouns' and that TWSI 'significantly beats all other sense inventories in the nouns-only rankings' (Section 6). This suggests the method is POS-dependent, but the paper provides no analysis of why or how to address this limitation.
evidence: Section 6: 'The area where our SubstClus inventories are weakest is in improving the lexsub rankings for nouns. The crowdsourced TWSI significantly beats all other sense inventories in the nouns-only rankings.'
Table 5: Nouns-only results show SubstClusCPWT Oracle GAP of 0.669 on Syn.VSM vs TWSI 0.756 (0.087 gap).
No analysis of why the method fails on nouns or how to improve it.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze why the method fails on nouns: (1) Are noun paraphrases less substitutable? (2) Is the Context Substitutability view less effective for nouns? (3) Are WordNet synsets for nouns less useful? (4) Conduct ablation by POS to identify which view(s) are problematic for nouns. (5) Consider POS-specific optimization or view weighting.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter sensitivity not explored
concerns.description: The paper makes several hyperparameter choices without sensitivity analysis: (1) PPDB score threshold of 2.3, (2) k range of 2-10 for cluster number selection, (3) λi=0.01 for all views, (4) β=0.5 for B3F, (5) 1000 sentences for Context Substitutability view. None of these choices are validated via sensitivity analysis.
evidence: Section 4.2: 'We chose 2.3 as the threshold score because it gave the best precision and recall when used as a threshold over the CoInCo training data.' No sensitivity analysis provided.
Section 4.2: 'For each target word to be clustered, we try clustering with a range of k between 2 and 10.' No justification for this range; no analysis of what happens outside this range.
Supplemental Material A.2: 'In the original paper and in our experiments, we set λi = 0.01 for all i.' No sensitivity analysis.
Supplemental Material A.1: 'In our work we use β = 0.5 to emphasize precision over recall in the substitutability score.' No justification or sensitivity analysis.
Section 3.1.1: '1000 in our experiments' for sentence sample size. No sensitivity analysis.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters: (1) Vary PPDB threshold (e.g., 2.0, 2.3, 2.5, 2.8) and report B3F and GAP. (2) Vary k range (e.g., 2-5, 2-10, 2-15) and report results. (3) Vary λi (e.g., 0.001, 0.01, 0.1) and report results. (4) Vary β (e.g., 0.25, 0.5, 1.0) and report B3F rankings. (5) Vary sentence sample size (e.g., 500, 1000, 2000) and report results.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing reported
concerns.description: The paper reports GAP improvements but does not provide confidence intervals, p-values, or statistical significance tests. It is unclear whether reported improvements are statistically significant or within noise margins.
evidence: Table 5: GAP scores reported without error bars or confidence intervals.
No mention of statistical significance testing (e.g., paired t-test, bootstrap confidence intervals).
Some improvements are small (e.g., SubstClusC on Syn.VSM: 0.520→0.576 best-fit, a 0.056 improvement or 10.8% relative gain).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute 95% confidence intervals for all GAP scores using bootstrap resampling (resample sentences with replacement). Report p-values for pairwise comparisons between sense inventories using paired t-tests or permutation tests. Clarify which improvements are statistically significant at α=0.05.

concerns.title: Coverage metrics not explicitly reported
concerns.description: The paper claims that SubstClus inventories have 'wider coverage' than existing sense inventories (Abstract, Section 4.3), but coverage metrics (number of target words, number of paraphrases with assigned senses) are not explicitly reported in the main results.
evidence: Abstract: 'They can be applied as a filter over lexical substitution rankings generated by existing vector- and embedding-based ranking models to significantly improve their performance.'
Section 4.3: 'all multi-view inventories and the SubstClusP single-view inventory are more substitutable than WordNet and TWSI in terms of B-Cubed F-Score.'
Table 2: Reports coverage for baseline inventories (WordNet+: 155K targets, TWSI: 1K targets, PPDBClus: 1.7M targets) but not for SubstClus inventories.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add a row to Table 2 reporting coverage metrics for each SubstClus inventory: (1) Number of target words with assigned senses, (2) Average number of paraphrases per target, (3) Total number of unique paraphrases. Compare to baselines to validate the 'wider coverage' claim.

concerns.title: Generalization to other lexsub datasets not evaluated
concerns.description: The paper evaluates the method only on CoInCo (327 target words). Generalization to other lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007, SemEval-2015) is not tested. This limits the external validity of the findings.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'We draw the target words for our clustering experiment from the Concepts In Context (CoInCo) dataset.'
Section 5.1: 'We use the test portion of the CoInCo subset defined in Section 4.1 to evaluate the extent to which our baseline and optimized sense inventories improve lexical substitution rankings.'
No mention of evaluation on SemEval-2007 or other standard lexsub benchmarks.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate the method on SemEval-2007 Lexical Substitution dataset and/or SemEval-2015 Paraphrase dataset. Report B3F and GAP scores on these external datasets to validate generalization. If performance differs significantly from CoInCo, investigate why.

concerns.title: Assumption that word sense is discrete and meaningful not validated
concerns.description: The paper assumes that word sense is a meaningful and discrete organizational principle for paraphrases (Assumption A1). However, this assumption is not validated. Modern linguistic theory recognizes that word senses exist on a continuum and that discrete sense boundaries are often arbitrary.
evidence: Section 2: 'A sense inventory, Ct, as a set of sets, {c1, c2, . . . ck}, where each subset contains synonyms of the target t corresponding to one of its senses.'
Table 1: Example assumes three discrete senses for 'paper', but the boundary between senses may be fuzzy.
No discussion of sense granularity or validation against gold sense inventories (e.g., WordNet).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate the discrete sense assumption by comparing automatically-induced clusters to WordNet synsets or other gold sense inventories. Compute agreement metrics (e.g., purity, NMI) to assess whether induced clusters align with human sense judgments. Discuss implications if senses are not discrete.

concerns.title: Silhouette Coefficient for cluster number selection may not align with substitutability
concerns.description: The paper uses Silhouette Coefficient (based on paraphrase-paraphrase matrix XP) to select the optimal number of clusters k. However, Silhouette Coefficient measures geometric cluster quality, not substitutability. It is unclear whether maximizing Silhouette Coefficient leads to maximizing substitutability (B3F).
evidence: Section 4.2: 'For each resulting clustering, we calculate the mean Silhouette Coefficient... We choose as the final clustering solution, that clustering which produces the highest Silhouette Coefficient.'
No analysis of correlation between Silhouette Coefficient and B3F across different k values.
Silhouette Coefficient is computed on XP (paraphrase similarity), but substitutability depends on all four views.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze the relationship between Silhouette Coefficient and B3F: (1) For each target word, compute Silhouette Coefficient and B3F for all k values (2-10). (2) Compute correlation between Silhouette Coefficient and B3F. (3) If correlation is weak, consider using B3F directly for k selection instead of Silhouette Coefficient.

concerns.title: AddCos model used for both clustering and evaluation
concerns.description: The Context Substitutability view uses AddCos scores to measure paraphrase fit in context. AddCos is also used as one of the ranking models for lexsub evaluation. This creates a potential circularity: the clustering is optimized using AddCos, and then AddCos is used to evaluate the clustering. This may bias results in favor of the AddCos ranking model.
evidence: Section 3.1.1: 'we choose to measure lexical substitutability using a simple but high-performing vector space model, AddCos.'
Section 5.2: 'The second model we use is the AddCos model introduced in section 3.1.1.'
Table 5: AddCos ranking results show similar or better performance than Syn.VSM for SubstClus inventories.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: To avoid circularity, consider using a different model (e.g., Syn.VSM) for the Context Substitutability view, or evaluate the clustering using a ranking model that was not used in clustering. Alternatively, report results separately for AddCos and Syn.VSM to assess whether the method is biased toward AddCos.

concerns.title: Best-fit WSD heuristic lacks justification and comparison to baselines
concerns.description: The best-fit WSD method (selecting the sense most frequently represented in top-5 ranked substitutes) is simple and heuristic. The paper provides no justification for why this particular heuristic should work, and does not compare it to more sophisticated WSD methods (e.g., Lesk algorithm, neural WSD models).
evidence: Section 5.4: 'For each target word in context, we choose the 'best-fit' sense to be the sense most frequently represented among the top-5 ranked substitutes by the lexsub ranking model.'
No justification for the top-5 window size or frequency-based selection.
No comparison to other WSD methods.
Section 6: 'The simple WSD method fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases; this is an area for improvement.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Justify the best-fit heuristic: (1) Conduct ablation on window size (e.g., top-3, top-5, top-10) and report results. (2) Compare to more sophisticated WSD methods (e.g., Lesk algorithm using WordNet, neural WSD models). (3) Analyze failure cases to understand when/why the heuristic breaks down. (4) Consider alternative WSD methods (e.g., maximum overlap, weighted voting).
