Method is heuristic (top-5 frequency); no justification for why this particular heuristic should work or comparison to alternative WSD methods.
Best-Fit GAP for PPDBClus is identical to oracle GAP (0.432 on Syn.VSM), suggesting the method may be biased toward certain sense inventory structures.
No statistical significance testing; unclear whether Best-Fit improvements are statistically significant or just noise.

identified_claims.claim_label: Sense filtering improves lexsub rankings across models
identified_claims.claim_text: Sense filtering using automatically-generated sense inventories can significantly improve lexical substitution rankings generated by existing vector- and embedding-based models (Syn.VSM, AddCos).
evidence: Table 5: Oracle GAP improvements across all sense inventories for both Syn.VSM and AddCos models; e.g., SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM: 0.520 unfiltered → 0.675 oracle (0.155 improvement).
Section 6: 'All baseline and clustered sense inventories can improve the GAP score of the Syn.VSM and AddCos ranking models when used as a filter, based on Oracle GAP scores.'
Table 4 example: sense filtering improves GAP from 0.47 to 0.78 for target 'year'.
uncertainty_flags: Oracle experiment assumes perfect sense knowledge; practical Best-Fit improvements are much smaller and inconsistent: e.g., SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM shows 0.520→0.552 best-fit (only 0.032 improvement, 6% relative gain).
Improvement magnitude varies widely by sense inventory and model: e.g., SubstClusC on Syn.VSM shows 0.520→0.641 oracle but 0.520→0.576 best-fit, a large gap.
PPDBClus shows poor Best-Fit performance (0.432 oracle, 0.432 best-fit on Syn.VSM), suggesting method is not universally applicable.
Claim of 'significant' improvement is not quantified; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported.
Best-Fit GAP for SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM (0.552) is lower than unfiltered baseline for some models, suggesting filtering can sometimes hurt performance.
Generalization to other lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007) is not evaluated; results may be specific to CoInCo.

strengths.title: Clear problem reformulation and motivation
strengths.description: The paper effectively reframes lexical substitution as a sense-filtering task, providing clear motivation through examples (Table 1) and literature review. The hypothesis that high-coverage, substitutable sense inventories can improve SOTA models is well-articulated and testable.
evidence: Introduction (lines 100-160) provides clear motivation with concrete examples of how sense affects substitutability.
Table 1 demonstrates the problem with three annotated sentences for 'paper' showing different sense clusters.
Section 7 literature review documents the shift from early two-step approaches to current SOTA models that ignore sense.

strengths.title: Methodologically sound multi-view integration
strengths.description: The multi-view NMF approach is well-designed, incorporating four complementary views (Context Substitutability, Paraphrase Similarity, WordNet Synsets, Shared Translations) that each provide independent signal for sense clustering. The technical implementation is sound and clearly described.
evidence: Sections 3.1.1-3.1.4 provide detailed descriptions of each view with clear motivation for why each view contributes to substitutability.
Section 3.1 explains multi-view NMF algorithm and its assumptions clearly.
Supplemental Material A.2 provides full technical details of the multi-view NMF implementation.

strengths.title: Comprehensive empirical evaluation with oracle baseline
strengths.description: The paper includes both oracle and practical experiments, providing a clear upper bound on performance and enabling assessment of the WSD method's effectiveness. The oracle experiment is well-designed and clearly demonstrates the potential of sense filtering.
evidence: Section 5.3-5.4 describes oracle and best-fit experimental setup clearly.
Table 5 provides comprehensive results across multiple sense inventories and ranking models.
Table 4 provides a concrete example of sense filtering with detailed step-by-step explanation.

strengths.title: Transparent reporting of limitations and POS-specific performance variation
strengths.description: The paper honestly acknowledges weaknesses, particularly the substantial gap between oracle and best-fit performance and the failure of the method on nouns. This transparency is valuable for readers assessing the practical applicability of the work.
evidence: Section 6: 'The simple WSD method fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases; this is an area for improvement.'
Section 6: 'The area where our SubstClus inventories are weakest is in improving the lexsub rankings for nouns.'
Section 6: 'The Best-Fit GAP scores are not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP scores, however, indicating that our simple WSD method may introduce bias.'

strengths.title: Task-specific metric design (B-Cubed F-Score for substitutability)
strengths.description: The application of B-Cubed F-Score to measure sense inventory fitness for lexsub is well-motivated and operationalized. The metric captures the notion of substitutability by measuring agreement between sense inventories and human annotations.
evidence: Section 2 provides clear motivation for why B-Cubed F-Score is appropriate for measuring substitutability.
Section 2.1 and Supplemental Material A.1 provide detailed implementation of the metric.
Table 2 shows B3F scores for multiple sense inventories, enabling comparison.

strengths.title: Ablation study showing view contributions
strengths.description: The paper experiments with seven different combinations of views (Section 4.2), providing evidence for the contribution of each view to clustering quality. This ablation helps validate the multi-view approach.
evidence: Section 4.2 describes the seven view combinations tested: C, P, W, T, CP, CPW, CPWT.
Table 5 shows results for all view combinations, enabling comparison of their contributions.
Figure 1 visualizes clustering results for different view combinations for the target 'slip.V'.

concerns.title: Unquantified correlation between B-Cubed F-Score and Oracle GAP
concerns.description: The paper claims that B-Cubed F-Score is 'generally a good indicator' of oracle GAP potential (Section 6), but provides no quantitative measure of this correlation (e.g., Pearson/Spearman coefficient, R-squared). This weakens the validity claim for the metric.
evidence: Section 6: 'Comparing the B-Cubed F-Score for the sense inventories to the Oracle GAP scores, we find that our substitutability metric is generally a good indicator of the potential for a sense inventory to improve lexsub rankings.' (No correlation coefficient provided.)
Table 2 and Table 5 show general alignment but no statistical measure of correlation.
Counterexample: PPDBClus has B3F of 0.736 (lower than WordNet+ 0.841 and TWSI 0.842) but achieves Oracle GAP of 0.432 on Syn.VSM, which is lower than expected if B3F were a strong predictor.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute and report Pearson/Spearman correlation coefficient between B3F scores and Oracle GAP scores across all sense inventories. Include 95% confidence intervals. If correlation is weak (r < 0.7), revise the claim about metric validity.

concerns.title: Substantial gap between oracle and best-fit performance not adequately addressed
concerns.description: The paper demonstrates oracle improvements of 0.12-0.16 GAP but best-fit improvements of only 0.03-0.06 GAP (Table 5). This 18% relative loss is substantial and undermines the practical applicability claim. The paper acknowledges the gap but does not adequately analyze or address it.
evidence: Table 5: SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM shows 0.675 oracle vs 0.552 best-fit, a 0.123 absolute difference (18% relative loss).
Table 5: SubstClusCPWT on AddCos shows 0.671 oracle vs 0.542 best-fit, a 0.129 absolute difference (19% relative loss).

Section 6: 'The Best-Fit GAP scores are not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP scores, however, indicating that our simple WSD method may introduce bias.' (Understatement of the magnitude of the gap.)
No error analysis or investigation of failure modes provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct detailed error analysis of the best-fit WSD method: (1) Analyze cases where best-fit sense selection fails; (2) Investigate whether the top-5 heuristic is appropriate or if alternative thresholds would improve performance; (3) Compare best-fit performance to more sophisticated WSD methods (e.g., Lesk algorithm, neural WSD); (4) Discuss whether the oracle-to-practical gap is inherent to the task or specific to the simple heuristic.

concerns.title: POS-specific performance variation not adequately analyzed
concerns.description: The paper reports that SubstClus inventories are 'weakest' on nouns (Section 6), with TWSI significantly outperforming all other inventories on nouns. This suggests the method is POS-dependent, but the paper does not investigate why or propose solutions.
evidence: Table 5: For nouns only, TWSI achieves 0.691 Best-Fit GAP on Syn.VSM, while SubstClusCPWT achieves only 0.555, a 0.136 gap.

Section 6: 'The area where our SubstClus inventories are weakest is in improving the lexsub rankings for nouns. The crowdsourced TWSI significantly beats all other sense inventories in the nouns-only rankings.'
Section 6: 'This suggests that performance in this task may be part-of-speech specific, and different optimization methods may be required for each part of speech.' (Acknowledged but not addressed.)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Investigate why the method fails on nouns: (1) Analyze the characteristics of noun sense inventories generated by SubstClus vs. TWSI (e.g., granularity, coverage); (2) Examine whether the Context Substitutability view is less effective for nouns; (3) Test whether different hyperparameters (e.g., k range, PPDB threshold) improve noun performance; (4) Consider POS-specific optimization or separate models for different POS.

concerns.title: Coverage metrics claimed but not reported
concerns.description: The abstract claims the method produces sense inventories with 'wider coverage' than existing inventories, but coverage metrics are not explicitly reported in the main results. Only CoInCo overlap is shown in Table 2, which does not directly measure the coverage of the full sense inventory.
evidence: Abstract: 'Our method results in sense clusters that are more substitutable and have wider coverage than existing sense inventories.'
Table 2: Only 'Avg CoInCo Overlap' is reported, not total coverage of the sense inventory.
No explicit reporting of total number of target words or paraphrases covered by SubstClus vs. baselines.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report coverage metrics for all sense inventories: (1) Total number of target words covered; (2) Total number of paraphrases covered; (3) Average number of paraphrases per target word; (4) Comparison to baselines (WordNet+, TWSI, PPDBClus). Include these metrics in Table 2 or a new table.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing for GAP improvements
concerns.description: The paper reports GAP scores but does not provide statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or p-values. It is unclear whether observed improvements are statistically significant or due to random variation.
evidence: Table 5 reports point estimates of GAP scores with no confidence intervals or significance tests.
No mention of statistical testing methodology in Section 5 or 6.
Best-Fit GAP improvements are often small (e.g., 0.032 for SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM), making significance testing particularly important.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct statistical significance testing: (1) Compute 95% confidence intervals for all GAP scores using bootstrap resampling; (2) Perform paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing SubstClus inventories to baselines; (3) Report p-values and effect sizes; (4) Discuss which improvements are statistically significant at α=0.05.

concerns.title: Unvalidated assumption of view complementarity
concerns.description: The multi-view NMF approach assumes that the four views are complementary and provide independent signal for sense clustering (Section 3.1). However, this assumption is not validated. The paper does not analyze correlations between views or provide evidence that they are truly complementary.
evidence: Section 3.1: 'Multi-view NMF assumes that the views are complementary, and that each view is likely to cluster the data the same way on its own.'
No correlation analysis between views provided.

Ablation results (Table 5) show mixed performance across view combinations, suggesting views may not be uniformly complementary: e.g., SubstClusC (0.641 oracle) outperforms SubstClusCP (0.681 oracle) on Syn.VSM, suggesting adding P view may not always help.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate the complementarity assumption: (1) Compute pairwise correlations between the four view matrices (XS, XP, XW, XF) for a sample of target words; (2) Analyze whether views provide redundant or independent information; (3) Investigate whether certain view combinations are more complementary than others; (4) Consider information-theoretic measures (e.g., mutual information) to quantify view independence.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter sensitivity not explored
concerns.description: The paper makes several hyperparameter choices (λi=0.01, β=0.5, k range 2-10, PPDB threshold 2.3, sample size 1000) but does not explore sensitivity to these choices. It is unclear how robust the results are to these parameters.
evidence: Section 4.2: 'We chose 2.3 as the threshold score because it gave the best precision and recall when used as a threshold over the CoInCo training data.' (No sensitivity analysis provided.)
Supplemental Material A.2: 'In the original paper and in our experiments, we set λi = 0.01 for all i.' (No justification or sensitivity analysis.)
Supplemental Material A.1: 'In our work we use β = 0.5 to emphasize precision over recall in the substitutability score.' (No justification or sensitivity analysis.)
Section 4.2: 'we try clustering with a range of k between 2 and 10' (No justification for this range or sensitivity analysis.)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: (1) Vary λi (e.g., 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0) and report impact on B3F and GAP scores; (2) Vary β (e.g., 0.25, 0.5, 1.0) and report impact on sense inventory rankings; (3) Vary k range (e.g., 2-5, 2-10, 2-15) and report impact on clustering quality; (4) Vary PPDB threshold (e.g., 2.0, 2.3, 2.5) and report impact on coverage and noise; (5) Vary sample size for Context Substitutability view (e.g., 500, 1000, 2000) and report impact on clustering quality.

concerns.title: Generalization to other lexsub datasets not evaluated
concerns.description: The paper evaluates the method only on the CoInCo dataset. Generalization to other lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007) is not tested, limiting the external validity of the results.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'We draw the target words for our clustering experiment from the Concepts In Context (CoInCo) dataset.'
Section 5.1: 'We use the test portion of the CoInCo subset defined in Section 4.1 to evaluate the extent to which our baseline and optimized sense inventories improve lexical substitution rankings.'
No mention of evaluation on SemEval-2007 or other lexsub datasets.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate the method on additional lexsub datasets: (1) Test on SemEval-2007 Lexical Substitution dataset; (2) Compare performance to baselines on this dataset; (3) Analyze whether results generalize or if performance is dataset-specific; (4) Discuss potential reasons for any differences in performance across datasets.

concerns.title: Simple WSD heuristic not compared to alternative methods
concerns.description: The paper uses a simple heuristic (best-fit sense selection from top-5 ranked substitutes) for WSD but does not compare it to more sophisticated WSD methods. This limits understanding of whether the poor practical performance is due to the heuristic or the sense inventories.
evidence: Section 5.4: 'For each target word in context, we choose the 'best-fit' sense to be the sense most frequently represented among the top-5 ranked substitutes by the lexsub ranking model.'
No comparison to other WSD methods (e.g., Lesk algorithm, neural WSD, supervised WSD).
Section 6: 'The simple WSD method fails to find the best sense cluster in many cases; this is an area for improvement.' (Acknowledged but not addressed.)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compare the simple WSD heuristic to alternative methods: (1) Implement Lesk algorithm using WordNet definitions; (2) Implement a neural WSD method (e.g., using contextualized embeddings); (3) Compare performance of all methods on the CoInCo test set; (4) Analyze whether more sophisticated WSD methods can close the oracle-to-practical gap; (5) Discuss the trade-off between WSD method complexity and practical applicability.

concerns.title: Best-Fit GAP sometimes lower than unfiltered baseline
concerns.description: In some cases, Best-Fit GAP is lower than the unfiltered baseline GAP, suggesting that sense filtering can sometimes hurt performance. This is not discussed or analyzed.
evidence: Table 5: SubstClusP on Syn.VSM shows unfiltered GAP 0.692 but Best-Fit GAP 0.540, a decrease of 0.152.
Table 5: SubstClusCP on Syn.VSM shows unfiltered GAP 0.681 but Best-Fit GAP 0.550, a decrease of 0.131.
No discussion of why filtering sometimes hurts performance or how to avoid this.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze cases where sense filtering hurts performance: (1) Identify which sense inventories and ranking models show performance degradation; (2) Investigate whether the best-fit WSD method is selecting incorrect senses; (3) Analyze whether the sense inventories are too coarse-grained or too fine-grained for certain targets; (4) Propose methods to detect when filtering is likely to hurt performance and avoid it.

comparable_works.relevance: Directly comparable prior work on clustering paraphrases by sense using spectral clustering on PPDB.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SubstClus improves upon PPDBClus by incorporating multiple views and optimizing for substitutability rather than paraphrase similarity alone. However, PPDBClus achieves lower B3F scores (0.736) than SubstClus inventories, and Best-Fit GAP performance is poor (0.432 on Syn.VSM).

comparable_works.relevance: Prior work on automatically clustering paraphrases by sense using different methods.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SubstClus extends this work by incorporating multiple complementary views and explicitly optimizing for substitutability. The paper does not provide direct performance comparison to Apidianaki et al. (2014).

comparable_works.relevance: Crowdsourced sense inventory for nouns, developed specifically with substitutability in mind.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: TWSI achieves higher B3F scores (0.842) than most SubstClus inventories and significantly outperforms SubstClus on nouns (0.691 Best-Fit GAP vs. 0.555 for SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM). This suggests that crowdsourced inventories may be superior for nouns.

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational work on multi-view non-negative matrix factorization, which SubstClus adapts for sense clustering.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SubstClus applies multi-view NMF to a new problem (sense clustering for lexsub) and incorporates task-specific views (Context Substitutability, Shared Translations). The core algorithm is not novel.

comparable_works.relevance: Lexical substitution ranking model used as one of the baseline ranking models and for computing Context Substitutability view.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SubstClus uses AddCos as a component of the clustering method and as a baseline ranking model. The paper demonstrates that sense filtering can improve AddCos rankings.

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational work on B-Cubed F-Score metric for cluster evaluation.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SubstClus applies B-Cubed F-Score to measure sense inventory fitness for lexsub. The metric is not novel, but its application to this task is.

uncertainty_flags: B-Cubed F-Score superiority does not guarantee lexsub performance improvement; Best-Fit GAP often substantially lower than Oracle GAP, indicating potential metric-task misalignment.
Correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP is stated as 'generally' good but not quantified; no statistical measure of correlation provided.
Coverage metrics ('wider coverage' claim in abstract) are not explicitly reported; only CoInCo overlap is shown, which does not directly measure full sense inventory coverage.
Performance on nouns is significantly weaker than TWSI, suggesting method is POS-dependent and not universally applicable despite claims of generalizability.
Simple WSD heuristic (best-fit sense selection) has substantial gap from oracle performance (18% relative loss on average), raising questions about practical applicability.
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported for GAP improvements; unclear whether improvements are statistically significant.
Multi-view NMF assumption of view complementarity is not validated; ablation results show mixed performance across view combinations.
Hyperparameter choices (λi=0.01, β=0.5, k range 2-10, PPDB threshold 2.3, sample size 1000) are not justified or subjected to sensitivity analysis.
Generalization to datasets beyond CoInCo not evaluated; results may be dataset-specific.
Simple WSD heuristic not compared to alternative WSD methods; unclear whether poor practical performance is due to heuristic or sense inventories.
Best-Fit GAP sometimes lower than unfiltered baseline, suggesting filtering can hurt performance; this is not analyzed.
Claim that SOTA models 'ignore word sense' may be overstated; contextualized embeddings may implicitly capture sense distinctions.
alternative_interpretations: The oracle-to-practical performance gap (18% relative loss) may indicate that the sense filtering approach is fundamentally limited by the difficulty of WSD, rather than a limitation of the sense inventories themselves. More sophisticated WSD methods might close this gap.

The POS-specific performance variation (weakness on nouns) may reflect differences in how nouns are represented in PPDB or differences in the nature of noun polysemy, rather than a fundamental limitation of the multi-view clustering approach.

The improvement in oracle GAP may be due to candidate set filtering (removing non-paraphrases from PPDB) rather than sense filtering per se. The paper does not isolate the contribution of sense filtering from candidate set filtering.

The B-Cubed F-Score metric may not be the right metric for measuring sense inventory fitness for lexsub. Alternative metrics (e.g., based on downstream task performance) might better capture the notion of substitutability.
The simple WSD heuristic (top-5 frequency) may be suboptimal; alternative heuristics (e.g., top-10 frequency, weighted frequency) might perform better.

The multi-view NMF approach may be overly complex; simpler clustering methods (e.g., single-view clustering on Context Substitutability alone) might achieve similar performance with less computational cost.
transparency_notes: The paper is generally transparent about limitations, acknowledging the gap between oracle and best-fit performance and the weakness on nouns. However, the magnitude of these limitations is sometimes understated (e.g., 18% relative loss is described as 'not perfectly correlated').
The paper does not discuss potential biases in the CoInCo dataset or how they might affect the results. For example, if CoInCo is biased toward certain POS or domains, the method may not generalize.
The paper does not discuss the computational cost of the multi-view NMF approach or how it scales to larger paraphrase databases.
The paper does not discuss the potential for sense inventories to introduce errors or noise that could hurt downstream applications.

The paper does not discuss the trade-off between sense inventory coverage and quality; the PPDB threshold of 2.3 reduces coverage to improve quality, but the impact of this trade-off is not quantified.
The paper does not discuss how the method would perform on other languages or whether the approach is language-agnostic as claimed.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper adapts existing techniques (multi-view NMF, B-Cubed F-Score) to a new problem context (sense clustering for lexsub). While the problem reformulation is novel and the multi-view approach is well-motivated, the core algorithmic contributions are incremental. The novelty lies primarily in the problem formulation and the systematic empirical validation, not in fundamental algorithmic or theoretical innovations.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the oracle-to-practical performance gap could be closed through more sophisticated WSD methods, the practical applicability of the approach would be significantly strengthened.
If the method could be extended to perform well on nouns (e.g., through POS-specific optimization), the claim of universal applicability would be more credible.
If the B-Cubed F-Score correlation with Oracle GAP could be quantified and shown to be strong (r > 0.8), the validity of the metric would be more convincing.
If the method could be shown to generalize to other lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007), the external validity of the results would be stronger.
If the multi-view complementarity assumption could be validated through correlation analysis, the theoretical foundation of the approach would be more solid.
If statistical significance testing showed that Best-Fit GAP improvements are statistically significant, the practical contribution would be more compelling.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper reformulates lexical substitution as a sense-filtering task (novel framing) and combines existing techniques (multi-view NMF, B-Cubed F-Score) in a new way. The contribution is primarily in the problem formulation and systematic empirical validation, not in fundamental algorithmic innovation. The multi-view NMF approach is adapted from Liu et al. (2013), and B-Cubed F-Score is from Amigó et al. (2009). The novelty is in the application to sense clustering for lexsub, which is a sensible but incremental extension of prior work.
evidence: Section 3.1 adapts multi-view NMF from Liu et al. (2013) without significant algorithmic modifications.
Section 2 applies B-Cubed F-Score from Amigó et al. (2009) to a new task.

The four views (Context Substitutability, Paraphrase Similarity, WordNet Synsets, Shared Translations) are well-motivated but not fundamentally novel; each view uses existing techniques (AddCos, PPDB2.0 Score, WordNet embeddings, translation probabilities).
The problem reformulation (lexsub as sense filtering) is novel and well-motivated, but the solution approach is a straightforward application of existing techniques.
uncertainty_flags: The novelty of the problem reformulation is somewhat limited; the idea that sense information could improve lexsub has been explored in prior work (e.g., early lexsub models used explicit sense disambiguation).
The multi-view approach is well-motivated but not fundamentally novel; multi-view clustering has been applied to many problems.
The practical applicability of the approach is limited by the oracle-to-practical performance gap, which may reduce the impact of the contribution.

novelty_lenses.lens: Disruptive novelty (fundamental reconceptualization or paradigm shift)
novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper does not propose a fundamental reconceptualization of the lexical substitution task or a paradigm shift in how sense information is used. The approach is a straightforward application of sense filtering to improve existing ranking models. While the problem reformulation is useful, it does not represent a fundamental change in how the field approaches lexical substitution. The paper does not challenge core assumptions about the nature of word sense or substitutability; instead, it accepts the standard notion of discrete word senses and proposes a method to cluster paraphrases accordingly.
evidence: The paper assumes word sense is a meaningful and discrete organizational principle (assumption A1), which is a standard assumption in NLP.
The approach does not propose new theoretical insights about word sense or substitutability; it applies existing clustering techniques to a new problem.
The paper does not challenge the assumption that SOTA lexsub models 'ignore' word sense; it accepts this premise and proposes a filtering approach.
The method is presented as an improvement to existing lexsub models, not as a fundamental reconceptualization of the task.
uncertainty_flags: The problem reformulation (lexsub as sense filtering) could be viewed as a modest reconceptualization, but it is not a fundamental paradigm shift.
The multi-view approach could be viewed as a novel way to integrate multiple sources of information, but multi-view clustering is an established technique.
The practical limitations of the approach (oracle-to-practical gap, POS-specific performance) suggest that the approach may not represent a significant advance over existing methods.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper presents a well-motivated problem reformulation and systematic empirical validation, with clear strengths in methodological design and transparency about limitations. However, significant concerns about the practical applicability of the approach (18% oracle-to-practical performance gap), unquantified metric validity (B3F correlation with Oracle GAP), POS-specific performance variation (weakness on nouns), and lack of statistical significance testing limit confidence in the contribution. The novelty is moderate (incremental combination of existing techniques), and the practical impact is unclear given the substantial gap between oracle and best-fit performance. The paper makes a solid methodological contribution but falls short of making a compelling case for practical applicability. Confidence is further reduced by the lack of generalization testing beyond CoInCo and the absence of comparison to more sophisticated WSD methods. The paper would be strengthened by addressing the oracle-to-practical gap, quantifying metric validity, and providing statistical significance testing.

consensus_findings: The paper presents a well-motivated problem reformulation: reframing lexical substitution as a sense-filtering task rather than direct ranking is coherent and addresses a real limitation of SOTA models that ignore explicit word sense.

Multi-view NMF clustering approach is methodologically sound: the four views (Context Substitutability, Paraphrase Similarity, WordNet Synsets, Shared Translations) are well-chosen and theoretically motivated, with clear technical implementation.

Oracle experiments demonstrate substantial potential: sense filtering improves GAP scores by 0.12-0.16 points across all sense inventories and ranking models, establishing an upper bound on performance.

Transparent reporting of limitations is a strength: the paper honestly acknowledges POS-specific performance variation (weakness on nouns), the gap between oracle and best-fit performance, and the failure of the simple WSD method in many cases.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation with multiple baselines: comparison to WordNet+, TWSI, and PPDBClus across B-Cubed F-Score and GAP metrics provides solid empirical grounding.

Substantial gap between oracle and practical performance undermines applicability claims: Best-Fit GAP is 18% lower than Oracle GAP on average (e.g., 0.675 oracle vs. 0.552 best-fit for SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM), indicating the simple WSD heuristic is a significant bottleneck.

B-Cubed F-Score correlation with Oracle GAP is not quantified: the paper claims the metric is 'generally a good indicator' but provides no Pearson/Spearman correlation coefficient, weakening the validity claim.

POS-dependent performance variation is substantial and unresolved: TWSI significantly outperforms SubstClus on nouns (0.691 vs. 0.555 Best-Fit GAP on Syn.VSM), suggesting the method is not universally applicable despite claims of generalizability.
disagreements: Novelty assessment differs across reviewers: Structure Analyst (reviewer_1) rates novelty as moderate-to-incremental with solid methodological contribution; Incremental Assessor (reviewer_3) emphasizes the problem reformulation as novel; Disruptive Assessor (reviewer_4) rates novelty as low-to-moderate, noting the approach is a straightforward application of existing techniques. All agree the novelty is incremental rather than disruptive.

Interpretation of 'approximates oracle performance' (Claim C4): Methodology Auditor (reviewer_2) and Claim Verifier (reviewer_5) interpret the 18% gap as evidence the claim is contradicted by results; Structure Analyst (reviewer_1) frames it as a limitation requiring deeper analysis. The paper's own language ('approximates') is arguably overstated given the magnitude of the gap.

Severity of unvalidated view complementarity assumption: Methodology Auditor (reviewer_2) rates this as moderate concern; Claim Verifier (reviewer_5) rates it as moderate; Disruptive Assessor (reviewer_4) rates it as minor. Ablation results (Table 5) show mixed performance, but disagreement exists on whether this constitutes evidence against complementarity or merely indicates complex interactions.

Practical applicability threshold: Structure Analyst (reviewer_1) and Methodology Auditor (reviewer_2) suggest the oracle-to-practical gap is substantial enough to undermine practical applicability claims; Incremental Assessor (reviewer_3) and Disruptive Assessor (reviewer_4) acknowledge the gap but frame it as a limitation of the WSD heuristic rather than the sense inventories themselves. Disagreement on whether the gap is inherent to the task or specific to the simple heuristic.
uncertainty_hotspots: Metric-task alignment: B-Cubed F-Score superiority does not guarantee lexsub performance improvement. Best-Fit GAP is often substantially lower than Oracle GAP, and the paper does not quantify the correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP. This raises fundamental questions about whether B3F is a valid proxy for lexsub task fitness.

WSD method effectiveness: The simple best-fit heuristic (top-5 frequency) is ad-hoc and not compared to more sophisticated WSD methods. The 18% oracle-to-practical gap could be due to the simplicity of the heuristic rather than limitations of the sense inventories. Without comparison to alternative WSD methods, it is unclear whether the gap is inherent to the task or specific to the chosen method.

POS-specific performance variation: The method is significantly weaker on nouns than on other POS, with TWSI substantially outperforming SubstClus. The paper does not investigate why this occurs or propose solutions. This raises questions about the generalizability of the approach and whether different optimization strategies are needed for different POS.

Generalization beyond CoInCo: The method is evaluated only on the CoInCo dataset. Generalization to other lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007) is not tested. It is unclear whether the results are specific to CoInCo characteristics or whether the method generalizes more broadly.

View complementarity assumption: The paper assumes the four views are complementary, but this is not validated. Ablation results show mixed performance across view combinations, with single-view SubstClusP sometimes outperforming multi-view combinations. The degree to which views are truly complementary vs. redundant is uncertain.

Coverage metrics: The abstract claims 'wider coverage' than existing inventories, but coverage metrics are not explicitly reported. Only CoInCo overlap is shown in Table 2. The actual coverage of SubstClus inventories relative to baselines is uncertain.

Statistical significance: No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for GAP improvements. Given the relatively small test set (2091 sentences for 327 target words), it is uncertain whether observed improvements are statistically significant or due to random variation.

Hyperparameter robustness: Multiple hyperparameter choices (PPDB threshold 2.3, k range 2-10, λᵢ=0.01, β=0.5, sample size 1000) are made without sensitivity analysis. It is uncertain how robust the results are to these choices or whether they are optimal.
model_diversity_effects: Structure Analyst (reviewer_1) emphasizes logical coherence and argument chain integrity, identifying gaps between metric validity (B3F superiority) and practical task performance (Best-Fit GAP). This role naturally highlights the disconnect between oracle and practical results.

Methodology Auditor (reviewer_2) focuses on reproducibility and validity, identifying unvalidated assumptions (view complementarity, hyperparameter choices) and missing statistical rigor (no significance testing). This role naturally emphasizes methodological gaps.

Incremental Novelty Assessor (reviewer_3) evaluates the contribution relative to prior work, noting that the paper adapts existing techniques (multi-view NMF, B-Cubed F-Score) to a new problem context. This role naturally frames the contribution as incremental rather than disruptive.

Disruptive Novelty Assessor (reviewer_4) evaluates whether the paper introduces fundamental conceptual innovation or paradigm shifts. This role naturally rates novelty as low-to-moderate, noting the approach is a straightforward application of existing techniques.

Claim Verifier (reviewer_5) synthesizes evidence for and against each claim, identifying where claims are overstated relative to evidence (e.g., 'approximates oracle performance' when gap is 18%). This role naturally produces a balanced assessment of claim validity.

Diversity effect: The five roles produce complementary perspectives. Structure Analyst identifies logical gaps; Methodology Auditor identifies methodological gaps; Novelty Assessors (incremental and disruptive) frame the contribution differently; Claim Verifier synthesizes evidence. Together, they provide a comprehensive assessment that no single role could produce alone.
meta_review.editor_guidance: The paper presents a solid methodological contribution with clear strengths (well-motivated problem reformulation, comprehensive empirical validation, transparent reporting of limitations) and significant weaknesses (substantial oracle-to-practical performance gap, unquantified metric validity, POS-specific performance variation, limited generalization testing). The core question for editorial decision is whether the practical applicability of the approach justifies publication given the 18% oracle-to-practical performance gap and the failure of the simple WSD method on nouns. Key considerations: (1) The oracle experiments establish that sense filtering has potential, but the practical applicability is limited by the simple WSD heuristic. More sophisticated WSD methods might close the gap, but this is not explored. (2) The B-Cubed F-Score metric is well-motivated but its correlation with Oracle GAP is not quantified, weakening the validity claim. (3) The POS-specific weakness on nouns is substantial and unresolved, suggesting the method is not universally applicable. (4) The evaluation is limited to CoInCo; generalization to other datasets is unclear. (5) No statistical significance testing is provided; it is unclear whether improvements are statistically significant. Recommendation: The paper is suitable for publication with major revisions addressing: (a) quantification of B3F-Oracle GAP correlation; (b) deeper analysis of the oracle-to-practical gap and comparison to more sophisticated WSD methods; (c) investigation of POS-specific performance variation; (d) statistical significance testing; (e) evaluation on additional lexsub datasets. The paper makes a meaningful contribution to the lexsub literature, but the practical impact is limited by the substantial gap between oracle and practical performance. The honest reporting of limitations is commendable and should be preserved in revision.
meta_review.author_guidance: The paper addresses an important problem (improving SOTA lexsub models through sense filtering) with a well-designed multi-view clustering approach. To strengthen the contribution and address reviewer concerns, consider the following revisions: (1) Quantify the correlation between B-Cubed F-Score and Oracle GAP using Pearson/Spearman coefficients. If correlation is weak, revise the claim about metric validity. (2) Conduct detailed error analysis of the best-fit WSD method: identify failure modes, analyze cases where filtering hurts performance, and compare to more sophisticated WSD methods (e.g., Lesk algorithm, neural WSD). This will help clarify whether the oracle-to-practical gap is inherent to the task or specific to the simple heuristic. (3) Investigate why the method fails on nouns: analyze sense inventory characteristics, test POS-specific optimization, and propose solutions. This will strengthen the generalizability claim. (4) Report statistical significance testing for all GAP improvements using bootstrap confidence intervals and paired t-tests. (5) Evaluate the method on additional lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007) to assess generalization. (6) Conduct hyperparameter sensitivity analysis for key parameters (PPDB threshold, k range, λᵢ, β) to demonstrate robustness. (7) Validate the view complementarity assumption through correlation analysis or information-theoretic measures. (8) Explicitly report coverage metrics (number of target words, number of paraphrases) to support the 'wider coverage' claim. These revisions will address the main concerns raised by reviewers and strengthen the empirical foundation of the paper.
transparency_report: The paper is generally transparent about limitations, explicitly acknowledging the gap between oracle and best-fit performance, the weakness on nouns, and the failure of the simple WSD method. This transparency is commendable and increases credibility.

The paper provides detailed technical descriptions of the multi-view NMF algorithm, B-Cubed F-Score metric, and experimental setup, supporting reproducibility. Supplemental material includes additional implementation details.

The paper does not discuss potential biases in the CoInCo dataset or how they might affect generalization. For example, if CoInCo is biased toward certain POS or domains, the method may not generalize.
The paper does not discuss computational complexity or scalability of the multi-view NMF approach. Runtime and memory requirements are not reported.
The paper does not discuss how the method would perform on other languages or whether the approach is language-agnostic as claimed in the introduction.

The paper does not discuss the trade-off between sense inventory coverage and quality. The PPDB threshold of 2.3 reduces coverage to improve quality, but the impact of this trade-off is not quantified.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts or ethical considerations, though the application (lexical substitution) is relatively benign.
The paper does not discuss whether SubstClus sense inventories will be made publicly available for future research, limiting the resource contribution.

The paper does not discuss the relationship between sense inventory size (number of senses per target word) and performance. Larger inventories (PPDBClus) have lower B3F but sometimes better Best-Fit GAP, suggesting a trade-off that is not explored.

The paper does not discuss the assumption that word senses are discrete and paraphrases within a sense are mutually substitutable. This assumption may not hold for all words or contexts, but is not validated.
epistemic_limits: Correlation between B-Cubed F-Score and Oracle GAP is stated qualitatively ('generally a good indicator') but not quantified. The strength and statistical significance of this relationship are unknown. This limits confidence in the validity of B3F as a task-specific metric.

The oracle-to-practical performance gap (18% relative loss) is substantial, but the paper does not determine whether this gap is inherent to the task (WSD is fundamentally difficult) or specific to the simple heuristic (more sophisticated WSD methods might close the gap). This limits understanding of the practical applicability of the approach.

POS-specific performance variation is documented (weakness on nouns), but the underlying causes are not identified. It is unclear whether the issue is data-related (CoInCo may have fewer noun examples), method-related (multi-view NMF may not be suitable for nouns), or metric-related (B3F may not be appropriate for nouns).

The paper evaluates the method only on CoInCo. Generalization to other lexsub datasets is unknown. The results may be specific to CoInCo characteristics (domain, sense distribution, annotation quality) and may not generalize to other datasets.

The multi-view complementarity assumption is not validated. The degree to which the four views provide independent vs. redundant signal is unknown. Ablation results show mixed performance, but the underlying reasons are not analyzed.
Hyperparameter sensitivity is not explored. The robustness of the results to variations in PPDB threshold, k range, λᵢ, β, and sample size is unknown. The results may be sensitive to these choices.

Statistical significance of GAP improvements is unknown. No confidence intervals or significance tests are provided. It is unclear whether observed improvements are statistically significant or due to random variation.
The simple WSD heuristic is not compared to alternative WSD methods. It is unknown whether more sophisticated WSD methods (e.g., Lesk algorithm, neural WSD) could close the oracle-to-practical gap.

The claim that SOTA lexsub models 'ignore word sense' is not fully validated. Contextualized embeddings (e.g., BERT, ELMo) may implicitly capture sense distinctions without explicit sense inventories. The paper does not test against such models.
Coverage metrics are not explicitly reported. The actual coverage of SubstClus inventories relative to baselines is unknown. The 'wider coverage' claim in the abstract is not quantified.

The relationship between sense inventory quality (B3F) and lexsub task performance (GAP) is not fully understood. Best-Fit GAP is 'not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP', indicating the metric may not be a reliable proxy for task performance.

The paper does not determine whether the improvements in oracle GAP are due to sense filtering per se or to other factors (e.g., candidate set filtering, re-ranking bias). The mechanism by which sense filtering improves performance is not fully isolated.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper proposes SubstClus, a multi-view NMF clustering method to automatically generate word sense inventories optimized for lexical substitution (lexsub). The core contribution is reframing lexsub as a sense-filtering task and demonstrating that multi-view clustering incorporating Context Substitutability, Paraphrase Similarity, WordNet Synsets, and Shared Translations can produce sense inventories with higher B-Cubed F-Score than existing resources (WordNet+, TWSI, PPDBClus). Oracle experiments show substantial potential (0.12–0.16 GAP improvements), but practical applicability is limited by a simple WSD heuristic that achieves only modest improvements (0.03–0.06 GAP, 18% relative loss from oracle). The paper is methodologically sound with transparent reporting of limitations, but critical gaps exist between metric-level claims (B3F superiority) and task-level performance (Best-Fit GAP substantially lower than Oracle GAP). Key unresolved issues include: (1) unquantified correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP, (2) substantial oracle-to-practical performance gap, (3) POS-specific weakness on nouns, (4) evaluation limited to CoInCo dataset, and (5) no statistical significance testing. The contribution is incremental (adapting established multi-view NMF to a new problem context) but coherent and well-executed within its scope.
strengths: Well-motivated problem reformulation: The paper effectively reframes lexsub as a sense-filtering task, providing clear motivation through examples (Table 1) and literature review. The hypothesis that high-coverage, substitutable sense inventories can improve SOTA models is explicit and testable.

Methodologically sound multi-view integration: The four views are well-chosen and theoretically motivated. Each view encodes a different signal relevant to substitutability (context, paraphrase strength, structured knowledge, cross-lingual signal), and the multi-view NMF framework is appropriate for combining them.

Comprehensive empirical validation with oracle baseline: The oracle experiment is well-designed to establish an upper bound on sense-filtering improvements, enabling separation of method limitations from WSD limitations. Table 5 provides comprehensive results across multiple sense inventories and ranking models.

Transparent reporting of limitations: The paper honestly acknowledges POS-specific performance variation (weakness on nouns), the gap between oracle and best-fit performance (18% relative loss), and the failure of the simple WSD method in many cases. This transparency strengthens credibility.

Task-specific metric design: B-Cubed F-Score is formally defined and applied consistently to measure sense inventory fitness for lexsub, grounding the metric in human substitutability judgments from CoInCo.

Reproducible experimental setup: The paper provides sufficient detail for reproduction (data splits, hyperparameter choices, implementation details in supplemental material), supporting reproducibility and enabling future work.
limitations: Substantial gap between oracle and practical performance undermines applicability claims: Best-Fit GAP is 18% lower than Oracle GAP on average (e.g., SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM: 0.675 oracle vs. 0.552 best-fit, a 0.123 absolute difference). The paper acknowledges this gap but does not adequately analyze failure modes or propose solutions. The simple WSD heuristic (top-5 frequency) is ad-hoc and not compared to more sophisticated WSD methods (e.g., Lesk algorithm, neural WSD). Without such comparison, it is unclear whether the gap is inherent to the task or specific to the chosen heuristic.

B-Cubed F-Score correlation with Oracle GAP is not quantified: The paper claims B3F is 'generally a good indicator' of oracle GAP potential (Section 6) but provides no Pearson/Spearman correlation coefficient, R-squared, or other statistical measure. This weakens the validity claim for the metric as a task-specific measure. Additionally, the paper states that 'Best-Fit GAP scores are not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP scores', indicating metric limitations in practical settings where WSD is required.

POS-dependent performance variation is substantial and unresolved: TWSI significantly outperforms SubstClus on nouns (0.691 Best-Fit GAP vs. 0.555 for SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM, a 0.136 gap). The paper identifies this weakness but does not investigate why it occurs or propose POS-specific solutions. This suggests the method is not universally applicable despite claims of generalizability to 'all parts of speech' (Introduction, line 180).

Evaluation limited to single dataset with no statistical significance testing: The method is evaluated only on CoInCo (327 target words). Generalization to other lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007, SemEval-2015) is not tested. Additionally, no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported for GAP improvements. Given the relatively small test set (2091 sentences), it is unclear whether observed improvements are statistically significant or due to random variation.
open_questions: Can the oracle-to-practical performance gap be closed through more sophisticated WSD methods? The simple best-fit heuristic achieves only 18% of the oracle improvement on average. Comparison to Lesk-style approaches, supervised WSD classifiers, or contextualized embeddings would clarify whether the gap is inherent to the task or specific to the chosen heuristic. What is the performance ceiling for practical sense filtering?

Why does the method fail specifically on nouns, and can this be addressed? TWSI significantly outperforms SubstClus on nouns (0.136 GAP gap). Is this due to differences in sense granularity, coverage, or the nature of noun polysemy? Would POS-specific optimization or separate models for different POS improve performance? How does this limitation affect the generalizability claim?

What is the quantitative correlation between B-Cubed F-Score and Oracle GAP? The paper claims B3F is 'generally a good indicator' but provides no correlation coefficient. If correlation is weak (r < 0.7), does this undermine the use of B3F as an optimization target? How sensitive are the relative rankings of sense inventories to the choice of β parameter in B3F?

Do the four views truly provide complementary signal, or are they redundant? Ablation results (Table 5) show mixed performance across view combinations, with single-view SubstClusP sometimes outperforming multi-view combinations (e.g., 0.692 vs. 0.681 on Syn.VSM unfiltered). What is the correlation between views? Are certain view combinations more complementary than others?

How robust are the results to hyperparameter choices? The paper makes several hyperparameter choices (PPDB threshold 2.3, k range 2-10, λᵢ=0.01, β=0.5, sample size 1000) without sensitivity analysis. How much do results change if these parameters are varied? Which hyperparameters have the largest effect on performance?
consensus_snapshot: The paper presents a well-motivated problem reformulation (lexsub as sense filtering) with clear motivation and systematic empirical validation.
Multi-view NMF clustering approach is methodologically sound, with four well-chosen views that are theoretically motivated and clearly implemented.
Oracle experiments demonstrate substantial potential for sense filtering (0.12–0.16 GAP improvements), establishing an upper bound on performance.
Transparent reporting of limitations (oracle-to-practical gap, POS-specific weakness, WSD method failures) is a significant strength that increases credibility.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation with multiple baselines (WordNet+, TWSI, PPDBClus) and two ranking models (Syn.VSM, AddCos) provides solid empirical grounding.
The contribution is incremental (adapting established multi-view NMF to sense clustering for lexsub) rather than disruptive, but coherent and well-executed within its scope.

source_trace: Claim C1 (SOTA models ignore sense but can be improved by filtering): Supported by Section 7 literature review documenting shift from early two-step approaches to current SOTA models; Table 5 oracle results showing all sense inventories improve GAP; Table 4 example showing concrete improvement (0.47→0.78 GAP for 'year'). Uncertainty: contextualized embeddings may implicitly capture sense distinctions; oracle improvements do not rule out alternative explanations (re-ranking bias, candidate set filtering).

Claim C2 (Multi-view clustering produces more substitutable sense clusters): Supported by Table 2 B3F scores showing SubstClus variants outperform WordNet+ and TWSI; Section 4.3 statement that 'all multi-view inventories...are more substitutable than WordNet and TWSI'; Table 5 Oracle GAP improvements. Uncertainty: B3F superiority does not translate to Best-Fit GAP improvements; coverage metrics not explicitly reported; performance on nouns weaker than TWSI; single-view SubstClusP sometimes outperforms multi-view combinations.

Claim C3 (B-Cubed F-Score is valid metric for sense inventory fitness): Supported by Section 2 metric definition and motivation; Section 6 statement that B3F is 'generally a good indicator' of Oracle GAP potential; Table 2 and Table 5 showing general alignment between B3F and Oracle GAP. Uncertainty: correlation not quantified; Best-Fit GAP 'not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP'; β=0.5 choice not justified; metric evaluated only on CoInCo.

Claim C4 (Simple WSD method approximates oracle performance): Supported by Section 5.4 description of best-fit heuristic; Section 6 statement that 'in most cases...sense inventories can improve GAP score when simple WSD method is applied'. Uncertainty: gap between Oracle and Best-Fit GAP is substantial (18% relative loss); method fails on nouns; no analysis of failure modes; no comparison to alternative WSD methods; heuristic choice (top-5 frequency) lacks justification.

Claim C5 (Sense filtering improves lexsub rankings across models): Supported by Table 5 Oracle GAP improvements across all inventories and models; Section 6 statement that 'All baseline and clustered sense inventories can improve GAP score'; Table 4 example (0.47→0.78 for 'year'). Uncertainty: oracle improvements do not guarantee practical improvements; Best-Fit improvements much smaller and inconsistent; PPDBClus shows poor Best-Fit performance; no statistical significance testing; generalization to other datasets not evaluated.

Assumption A1 (Word sense is meaningful and discrete): Supported by Introduction examples (Table 1) and Section 2 definition of sense inventory as 'set of sets'. Uncertainty: assumption not validated against gold sense inventories; modern linguistic theory recognizes fuzzy sense boundaries; discrete sense assumption may not hold for all words.

Assumption A3 (Four views are complementary): Stated in Section 3.1 as core assumption of multi-view NMF. Uncertainty: assumption not validated; ablation results show mixed performance; single-view SubstClusP sometimes outperforms multi-view combinations; no correlation analysis between views provided.

Assumption A6 (Silhouette Coefficient maximization selects correct number of senses): Stated in Section 4.2 as method for choosing k. Uncertainty: no validation that Silhouette Coefficient correlates with true sense granularity; true number of senses may fall outside [2,10] range; no comparison to gold sense inventories.

Assumption A7 (Best-fit WSD heuristic approximates oracle performance): Stated in Section 5.4. Uncertainty: gap between Oracle and Best-Fit GAP is substantial (18% relative loss); method fails on nouns; no comparison to more sophisticated WSD methods; heuristic choice lacks justification.

Evaluation target: Substitutability metric validity (Section 6): Correlation between B3F and Oracle GAP stated as 'generally good' but not quantified. No Pearson/Spearman coefficient provided. This is a critical gap in the empirical validation.

Evaluation target: Sense inventory coverage (not explicitly reported): Abstract claims 'wider coverage' but Table 2 shows only 'Avg CoInCo Overlap', not total coverage. Coverage metrics should include total number of target words and paraphrases covered by each inventory.

Evaluation target: Practical applicability (Table 5, Section 6): Best-Fit GAP substantially lower than Oracle GAP (18% relative loss on average). Gap is acknowledged but not adequately analyzed. No comparison to more sophisticated WSD methods to establish performance ceiling.

Evaluation target: POS-specific performance (Table 5, Section 6): TWSI significantly outperforms SubstClus on nouns (0.691 vs. 0.555 Best-Fit GAP on Syn.VSM). Weakness is acknowledged but not investigated or addressed.

Evaluation target: Statistical significance (Table 5): No confidence intervals, p-values, or significance tests reported. Given small test set (2091 sentences), statistical testing is important but absent.
transparency_notes: The paper is generally transparent about limitations, explicitly acknowledging the gap between oracle and best-fit performance, the weakness on nouns, and the failure of the simple WSD method. This transparency is commendable and increases credibility.

The paper provides detailed technical descriptions of the multi-view NMF algorithm, B-Cubed F-Score metric, and experimental setup, supporting reproducibility. Supplemental material includes additional implementation details.

The paper does not discuss potential biases in the CoInCo dataset or how they might affect generalization. For example, if CoInCo is biased toward certain POS or domains, the method may not generalize.
The paper does not discuss computational complexity or scalability of the multi-view NMF approach. Runtime and memory requirements are not reported.
The paper does not discuss how the method would perform on other languages or whether the approach is language-agnostic as claimed in the introduction.

The paper does not discuss the trade-off between sense inventory coverage and quality. The PPDB threshold of 2.3 reduces coverage to improve quality, but the impact of this trade-off is not quantified.
The paper does not discuss whether SubstClus sense inventories will be made publicly available for future research, limiting the resource contribution.

The paper does not discuss the relationship between sense inventory size (number of senses per target word) and performance. Larger inventories (PPDBClus) have lower B3F but sometimes better Best-Fit GAP, suggesting a trade-off that is not explored.

The paper does not discuss the assumption that word senses are discrete and paraphrases within a sense are mutually substitutable. This assumption may not hold for all words or contexts, but is not validated.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: The paper presents a solid methodological contribution with clear strengths (well-motivated problem reformulation, comprehensive empirical validation, transparent reporting of limitations) and significant weaknesses (substantial oracle-to-practical performance gap, unquantified metric validity, POS-specific performance variation, limited generalization testing). The core question for editorial decision is whether the practical applicability of the approach justifies publication given the 18% oracle-to-practical performance gap and the failure of the simple WSD method on nouns. Key considerations: (1) The oracle experiments establish that sense filtering has potential, but the practical applicability is limited by the simple WSD heuristic. More sophisticated WSD methods might close the gap, but this is not explored. (2) The B-Cubed F-Score metric is well-motivated but its correlation with Oracle GAP is not quantified, weakening the validity claim. (3) The POS-specific weakness on nouns is substantial and unresolved, suggesting the method is not universally applicable. (4) The evaluation is limited to CoInCo; generalization to other datasets is unclear. (5) No statistical significance testing is provided; it is unclear whether improvements are statistically significant. Recommendation: The paper is suitable for publication with major revisions addressing: (a) quantification of B3F-Oracle GAP correlation; (b) deeper analysis of the oracle-to-practical gap and comparison to more sophisticated WSD methods; (c) investigation of POS-specific performance variation; (d) statistical significance testing; (e) evaluation on additional lexsub datasets. The paper makes a meaningful contribution to the lexsub literature, but the practical impact is limited by the substantial gap between oracle and practical performance. The honest reporting of limitations is commendable and should be preserved in revision.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: The paper addresses an important problem (improving SOTA lexsub models through sense filtering) with a well-designed multi-view clustering approach. To strengthen the contribution and address reviewer concerns, consider the following revisions: (1) Quantify the correlation between B-Cubed F-Score and Oracle GAP using Pearson/Spearman coefficients. If correlation is weak, revise the claim about metric validity. (2) Conduct detailed error analysis of the best-fit WSD method: identify failure modes, analyze cases where filtering hurts performance, and compare to more sophisticated WSD methods (e.g., Lesk algorithm, neural WSD). This will help clarify whether the oracle-to-practical gap is inherent to the task or specific to the simple heuristic. (3) Investigate why the method fails on nouns: analyze sense inventory characteristics, test POS-specific optimization, and propose solutions. This will strengthen the generalizability claim. (4) Report statistical significance testing for all GAP improvements using bootstrap confidence intervals and paired t-tests. (5) Evaluate the method on additional lexsub datasets (e.g., SemEval-2007) to assess generalization. (6) Conduct hyperparameter sensitivity analysis for key parameters (PPDB threshold, k range, λᵢ, β) to demonstrate robustness. (7) Validate the view complementarity assumption through correlation analysis or information-theoretic measures. (8) Explicitly report coverage metrics (number of target words, number of paraphrases) to support the 'wider coverage' claim. These revisions will address the main concerns raised by reviewers and strengthen the empirical foundation of the paper.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper proposes SubstClus, a multi-view NMF clustering method to automatically generate word sense inventories optimized for lexical substitution. The core argument is that current SOTA lexsub models ignore word sense but can be improved by filtering with high-quality sense inventories. The paper combines four complementary views (Context Substitutability, Paraphrase Similarity, WordNet Synsets, Shared Translations) and evaluates using B-Cubed F-Score as a substitutability metric and GAP as a lexsub performance metric. Oracle experiments show substantial improvements (0.12–0.16 GAP), but practical improvements using a simple WSD heuristic are modest (0.03–0.06 GAP, 18% relative loss from oracle).

Strengths:
- Well-motivated problem reformulation: The paper effectively reframes lexsub as a sense-filtering task, providing clear motivation through examples and literature review. The hypothesis is explicit and testable.
- Methodologically sound multi-view integration: The four views are well-chosen and theoretically motivated. Each view encodes a different signal relevant to substitutability, and the multi-view NMF framework is appropriate for combining them.
- Comprehensive empirical validation: The oracle experiment is well-designed to establish an upper bound on performance. Table 5 provides comprehensive results across multiple sense inventories and ranking models.
- Transparent reporting of limitations: The paper honestly acknowledges POS-specific performance variation (weakness on nouns), the gap between oracle and best-fit performance, and the failure of the simple WSD method. This transparency strengthens credibility.
- Task-specific metric design: B-Cubed F-Score is formally defined and applied consistently to measure sense inventory fitness for lexsub, grounding the metric in human substitutability judgments.
- Reproducible experimental setup: The paper provides sufficient detail for reproduction (data splits, hyperparameter choices, implementation details in supplemental material).

Limitations:
- Substantial gap between oracle and practical performance undermines applicability claims: Best-Fit GAP is 18% lower than Oracle GAP on average (e.g., SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM: 0.675 oracle vs. 0.552 best-fit). The paper acknowledges this gap but does not adequately analyze failure modes or propose solutions. The simple WSD heuristic is ad-hoc and not compared to more sophisticated WSD methods. Without such comparison, it is unclear whether the gap is inherent to the task or specific to the chosen heuristic.
- B-Cubed F-Score correlation with Oracle GAP is not quantified: The paper claims B3F is 'generally a good indicator' of oracle GAP potential but provides no Pearson/Spearman correlation coefficient. This weakens the validity claim for the metric. Additionally, the paper states that 'Best-Fit GAP scores are not perfectly correlated with Oracle GAP scores', indicating metric limitations in practical settings.
- POS-dependent performance variation is substantial and unresolved: TWSI significantly outperforms SubstClus on nouns (0.691 Best-Fit GAP vs. 0.555 for SubstClusCPWT on Syn.VSM). The paper identifies this weakness but does not investigate why or propose solutions, suggesting the method is not universally applicable despite claims of generalizability.
- Evaluation limited to single dataset with no statistical significance testing: The method is evaluated only on CoInCo (327 target words). Generalization to other lexsub datasets is not tested. Additionally, no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported for GAP improvements. Given the relatively small test set (2091 sentences), it is unclear whether observed improvements are statistically significant.

Open Questions:
- Can the oracle-to-practical performance gap be closed through more sophisticated WSD methods? The simple best-fit heuristic achieves only 18% of the oracle improvement on average. Comparison to Lesk-style approaches, supervised WSD classifiers, or contextualized embeddings would clarify whether the gap is inherent to the task or specific to the chosen heuristic.
- Why does the method fail specifically on nouns, and can this be addressed? TWSI significantly outperforms SubstClus on nouns (0.136 GAP gap). Is this due to differences in sense granularity, coverage, or the nature of noun polysemy? Would POS-specific optimization improve performance?
- What is the quantitative correlation between B-Cubed F-Score and Oracle GAP? The paper claims B3F is 'generally a good indicator' but provides no correlation coefficient. If correlation is weak, does this undermine the use of B3F as an optimization target?
- Do the four views truly provide complementary signal, or are they redundant? Ablation results show mixed performance across view combinations, with single-view SubstClusP sometimes outperforming multi-view combinations. What is the correlation between views?
- How robust are the results to hyperparameter choices? The paper makes several hyperparameter choices without sensitivity analysis. How much do results change if these parameters are varied?

Transparency:
The paper is generally transparent about limitations, explicitly acknowledging the gap between oracle and best-fit performance, the weakness on nouns, and the failure of the simple WSD method. The paper provides detailed technical descriptions and supplemental material supporting reproducibility. However, the paper does not discuss potential biases in the CoInCo dataset, computational complexity, language-agnostic claims, coverage-quality trade-offs, or whether sense inventories will be made publicly available. The assumption that word senses are discrete and paraphrases within a sense are mutually substitutable is not validated.

Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 🆕 ACL policy on great and irresponsible reviewers & chairs
Codes: I1, I12
Applies To: meta_reviewer, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, policy_screen, structure_analyst
Content: eview earlier and ask more experienced people in your network for feedback. Some ACs may also offer feedback for reviews that come in good time. Irresponsible reviewers and chairs. Unfortunately, with the growing number of conference submissions, there have been more and more cases where reviewers or chairs sign up for service and then simply disappear without a warning, are late without a warning, or submit (meta-)reviews that are completely unacceptable in their quality (e.g. extremely terse, unprofessional in tone, LLM-generated). Starting in October 2024, ARR provided the authors with the opportunity to report common issues with reviews (e.g. rude reviews, ‘not novel’ criticism without providing references, etc.) The ACs will see such reports, if any, judge their merit, and take them into account when writing the meta-review. A similar functionality has now been developed for meta-reviews, with author issue reports viewable for senior area chairs. Since the reviewer and AC guidelines may also seen by the authors during the response period, some sections of these guidelines now have codes for (meta-)review issues (I1-I12) that can be reported by the authors. More details here and here. Starting in May 2025, ARR also adopts the new policy on the ‘highly irresponsible’ (meta-)reviewers. The program chairs and ARR EiCs will consider the egregious cases reported by chairs (on their own judgement or based on author reports), including the cases of extremely terse reviews, unprofessional tone, and LLM-generated reviews.

Codes: I1, I12
